blocks.text: *Leadership and followership* is a free badged course of 8 weeks, with approximately 3 hours' study time each week. You can work through it at your own pace, so if you have more time one week there is no problem with pushing on to another week's study.

You'll start by considering your own leadership experience and learning about different leadership styles. You'll then focus on key leadership skills and how to develop them, explore good and bad leadership and possible solutions to problems, find out what makes a good follower and how leaders develop their followers, look at common leadership challenges and the future of leadership, and finally devise a plan to build your own experience.

pages.title: What you will be able to do

blocks.text: After completing this course, you should be able to:

items: describe a variety of leadership styles and approaches and analyse how they fit with personal preferences
recognise the skills required for leadership and assess personal experience and capability
define followership, from the perspectives of both the leader and the follower
identify how effective leadership can overcome a variety of common challenges
reflect on personal experience, start a leadership journal and devise an appropriate plan of action to develop leadership skills

blocks.text: Each week ends with a summary and a short quiz. The course has also been included in the National Careers Service skills toolkit to help you develop new skills.

pages.title: Week 1: Where are you starting from?

blocks.text: Welcome to Week 1. Both leadership and followership have been extensively researched by academics and business experts. This course is an introduction, combining practical advice with a taste of that research; references support further reading if you want to go deeper.

Reflection is an important part of your development as a leader, so you'll find many reflective activities throughout the course to help you build this skill. You may also find it useful to make notes as you go, or keep a notebook beside you as you study.

blocks.title: Introduction to Week 1
blocks.note: Lynne Johnson welcomes you to the course. You'll focus on key leadership skills and how to develop them, explore good and bad leadership and solutions to challenges, and learn what makes a good follower and how leaders can develop followers to create more productive relationships and encourage them towards future leadership roles. Finally you'll plan how to build your own experience. This week starts with your own leadership experience and identifying your aims, to help you get the most from the course.

blocks.text: By the end of this week, you will be able to:

items: recognise different definitions of leadership and followership
describe some of the differences and similarities between leadership and management
review and reflect on your own leadership experiences and aspirations
schedule time in your diary for these activities and use this time effectively

blocks.text: Leadership is a topic that people choose to study for a variety of reasons, including to:

items: enhance our personal leadership experience
further our theoretical understanding of leadership
enable us to develop more effective leaders within our organisations

blocks.text: Followership is closely linked with leadership, and the two concepts are now widely considered to be **interdependent** in producing successful outcomes for both individuals and businesses.

blocks.caption: Figure 1 Leader and followers

blocks.text: How would you describe leadership? Before looking at some definitions, consider what leadership means to you. *Allow about 10 minutes.*

blocks.title: Activity 1 What is a leader?
blocks.prompt: Think about leaders you are aware of, either from the media or from your own experience. What do they do every day? What are they needed for? What type of people are they? Write a sentence or paragraph that captures your view of what a leader is.
blocks.model: You could have approached this in different ways. Did you focus on the personal skills and qualities required by a leader, or on the process or tasks of leadership? These perspectives reflect the different ways researchers have conceptualised leadership. Your personal definition is a starting point: revisit it at the end of the course to see if you would change or add anything.
points: A leader influences or guides other people towards a goal.
Leadership can be described by personal skills, qualities or traits of the leader.
Leadership can also be described as a process or set of tasks, such as setting direction.
Leaders are needed to coordinate, motivate or make decisions for a group.

blocks.text: In *Leadership Theory and Practice*, Professor Peter Northouse takes the central components from 65 different classifications of leadership and distils them into this definition:
Leadership is a process whereby an individual influences a group of individuals to achieve a common goal.
Yet, as leadership expert Ralph Stogdill once wrote:
There are almost as many different definitions of leadership as there are persons who have attempted to define the concept.
Bret Bogenschneider (2016) presents an impressive list of definitions in his search for a common framework. It includes:

items: the process (act) of influencing the activities of an organised group in its efforts toward goal setting and goal achievement (Stogdill)
interpersonal influence, exercised in a situation and directed, through the communication process, toward the attainment of a specific goal or goals (Tannenbaum, Weschler and Massik)
when persons engage with others in such a way that leaders and followers raise one another to higher levels of motivation and morality (Burns)
those who consistently make effective contributions to social order, and who are expected and perceived to do so (Hosking)
typically defined by the traits, qualities and behaviours of a leader (Horner)

blocks.text: There are clear parallels between many of these definitions: **influence** is a common theme. But there are key differences in concept, with some authors describing leadership as a *process* and others highlighting *behaviours*.
Each writer's subject specialism (psychology, management or even statistics) also has an influence, along with the prevailing attitudes of the era in which the term was defined.

In more recent times, Northouse (2022) describes a growth in 'moral approaches to leadership' and, aligned with increasing awareness of the value of diversity in the workplace, the introduction of **inclusive leadership**, which you'll explore in Week 2.

blocks.q: What is the common theme running through most definitions of leadership?
blocks.explain: Most definitions describe leadership in terms of influencing others towards a goal, although they differ on whether it is a process, a behaviour or a set of traits.

blocks.text: Research on followership began in the 1950s, but didn't generate significant interest until 1988, with the work of Robert Kelley (you'll meet his work in Week 5). Early research focused on followers as passive participants. Now a growing body of research presents leadership as a shared endeavour between interdependent followers and leaders.
Crossman and Crossman (2011) reviewed the literature on followership. They cite authors with **leader-centred** views, for example:

items: the ability to effectively follow the directives and support the efforts of a leader to maximise a structured organisation (Bjugstad et al.)

a process in which subordinates recognise their responsibility to comply with the orders of leaders and take appropriate action consistent with the situation to carry out those orders to the best of their ability (Townsend and Gebhart)

blocks.text: These leader-centred definitions appear alongside more **follower-centred** perspectives, such as:

items: the process of attaining one's individual goals by being influenced by a leader into participating in individual or group efforts toward organisational goals in a given situation; followership becomes a function of the follower, the leader and situational variables (Wortman)
a relational role in which followers have the ability to influence leaders and contribute to the improvement and attainment of group and organisational objectives (Carsten et al.)

blocks.text: More recently, Pietraszewski (2020) suggests that no one individual has enough information to solve a complex problem alone. Leaders and followers are information-processing roles within a 'social marketplace, in which leaders propose possible coordination and cooperation enterprises, and followers evaluate and choose among these offered possibilities'.
Rebecca Fielding, Managing Director of Gradconsult, defines followership from the perspective of an employer.

blocks.title: What is followership?
blocks.note: Rebecca Fielding: followership is the act of implementing what an organisation requires of you - following and contributing to your peers, colleagues and the organisation. It is what 80 per cent of people in an organisation do every day: they make things happen and are trusted and relied upon to deliver. It matters because every leader was a fantastic follower first, and followers deliver for clients and customers, make the products and deliver the services. 'Fantastic followership is what business is all about.'

blocks.text: We are all followers, but what we gain from that relationship varies widely with our reasons for following, our enthusiasm for the leader's methods and goals, and our own skills and characteristics.

blocks.title: Activity 2 Who do you follow?
blocks.prompt: Write a list of the leaders you follow and your reasons for following them, in the workplace or virtually through social media. Consider: Is your 'followership' experience positive or negative? How does it affect you as a follower? What is your relationship with the leader? How does being a follower help you reach your own goals?
blocks.model: You'll explore followership in Week 5 from the perspectives of both follower and leader. You'll learn how important it is for a leader to support and develop their followers, how important good followers are in achieving a leader's vision, and the interdependence between followers and leaders in reaching positive outcomes for individuals and businesses.
points: Names specific leaders followed and the reasons for following them.
Judges whether the followership experience is positive or negative and how it affects them.
Describes the relationship with the leader.
Links following the leader to reaching their own goals.

blocks.text: The themes of this course are not as easily defined as you might have thought! Their complexity is what makes them interesting; this course simplifies some of it by giving a practical, real-life context.

pages.title: 2 Are leadership and management different or the same?

blocks.text: Authors, business experts, academics and practitioners give contrasting answers to this question. Some think the two roles are different, and others believe they are the same.

blocks.alt: Dilbert cartoon. A manager asks why it is taking so long to fix the control management system; Dilbert says the manager's leadership has taught him to give laughably unrealistic timelines and blame others when he misses deadlines; the manager replies 'You're not even doing that right', and Dilbert says 'I guess I need more of your leadership.'
blocks.caption: Figure 2 Managers and leaders in discussion

pages.title: Activity 3 Your views of leadership and management

blocks.text: Before looking at the different views in the literature: what is your opinion or experience of leadership and management? *Allow about 5 minutes.*

blocks.title: Activity 3 Your views of leadership and management
blocks.prompt: Write some words (e.g. focusing on tasks and competencies) that you associate with successful (a) leadership and (b) management. Write whatever comes into your head without thinking too long about it.
blocks.model: Did you find you could make a clear distinction between leadership and management, or did you write similar or overlapping terms? Does that come from your personal experience or observation of individuals in those roles?
points: Lists words for leadership such as vision, inspiring, influencing, direction.
Lists words for management such as planning, organising, controlling, processes.
Notices where the two lists differ or overlap.
Relates the words to personal experience or observation.

blocks.text: Many authors distinguish leadership and management as two separate functions, both crucial to organisational success:

items: **Zaleznik (1977)**: 'managers embrace process, seek stability and control, and instinctively try to resolve problems quickly - sometimes before they fully understand a problem's significance. Leaders, in contrast, tolerate chaos and lack of structure and are willing to delay closure in order to understand the issues more fully.'

**Kotter (1990)**: management is about planning, organising and controlling, while leadership involves establishing direction, aligning and motivating people. This is too much for one person, so separate roles are needed if organisations are to flourish.

blocks.text: Drawing on the research of Warren Bennis, Roger Gill (2006, p. 27) summarises the differences:

head: The manager
The leader
rows: Is his or her own person

blocks.text: *Table 1 The differences between management and leadership (Source: Gill, 2006, p. 27)*
Other experts contend that management and leadership may involve different skills and processes, but needn't be done by separate people, and that separating them can even damage an organisation:

items: **Morgan Witzel (2013)**: 'we have managers who cannot and will not lead, because they believe that leadership is someone else's responsibility' and 'at the other end of the spectrum, we have a cadre of leaders who believe management is beneath them.'

**Tyler (2007)**: 'management involves far more than planning, implementation and the exercise of co-ordination and control'; 'Leadership - the ability to communicate a vision, influence others and gain their trust - will be crucial to achieving your objectives as a manager, and in turn, those of the organisation.'
The **POLC framework**, a management tool, categorises the four principal functions of management as Planning, Organising, Leading and Controlling.

blocks.text: Debate will continue, but there are clearly elements of a leader's and a manager's role that overlap. This course focuses on leadership skills and processes, which may be relevant to people in either leadership or management roles, depending on their job descriptions.
Theoretical frameworks underpin the work of an effective leader. Next you'll reflect on your practical leadership experience before looking at how theory might influence your further development.

blocks.q: Kotter (1990) argues that one person can comfortably combine all leadership and management functions.
blocks.explain: Kotter says planning, organising and controlling (management) plus establishing direction, aligning and motivating (leadership) is too much for one person, so separate roles are needed.

blocks.title: Match each view to its author or framework

pairs.def: Managers seek stability and control; leaders tolerate chaos and delay closure to understand issues
Management plans, organises and controls; leadership sets direction, aligns and motivates - separate roles are needed
The manager does things right; the leader does the right thing
Some managers won't lead and some leaders think management is beneath them
Communicating a vision, influencing and gaining trust is crucial to achieving a manager's objectives
Planning, Organising, Leading and Controlling as the four functions of management

blocks.text: Reviewing your own leadership experience gives you a personal starting point for this course and a clearer idea of what to do next. You might have developed leadership skills by:

items: taking a leadership role in the workplace for a project or team
organising a fundraising event or social gathering
mentoring someone
volunteering to lead a project or group in your local community
taking responsibility at home due to the illness of a parent or guardian
being captain of a sports team
holding a committee position in a university society
leading a group project as part of your course

blocks.alt: Word cloud with words such as leadership, management, team, trust, integrity, creativity, innovation, risk, experience and vision
blocks.caption: Figure 3 Key words that capture the essence of leadership

blocks.text: Rebecca Fielding adds her ideas about ways to build your leadership experience both within and outside the workplace.

blocks.title: Building your leadership experience
blocks.note: Rebecca Fielding: you can build leadership experience before work - volunteering, getting involved in projects, offering to lead a piece of group work as a student, joining a club or society and taking a role (not necessarily captain - treasurer or membership director count too), helping at a church, mosque, sports or youth group, school or library. 'Putting your hand up' - volunteering to take responsibility and make something happen, taking a risk and learning as you go - is the fundamental essence of leadership. Some of the best leaders are thoughtful, quiet people in the background. At work, if you see something that needs doing, offer to do it or simply do it; join employability or employee voice groups, committees and extra projects, and make little differences every day.

blocks.text: You don't have to be a 'rabble rouser' to lead. Volunteering to take responsibility - 'putting your hand up' - is where leadership starts.

blocks.title: Activity 4 Reviewing your leadership experience
blocks.prompt: Note any occasion, role or activity that has involved you leading in some way (if you were part of a leadership group, think about your specific role). For each example ask: If you asked the others involved who was the leader, would they say it was you? Did you consciously decide to lead or did the situation evolve around you? Did you enjoy being the leader? Looking back, could you have done anything differently?
blocks.model: The context may have coloured your perception: if it felt negative or forced on you, you may underestimate how much you learned, so try to detach your emotions and view it analytically. If you expected to fail but surprised yourself, look for a new experience that pushes you further. If you felt disappointed, think about why and whether others would agree. Don't worry if you don't have many examples yet. Asking whether you would do anything differently is a useful learning tool.
points: Describes at least one concrete leadership occasion or role.
Considers whether others saw them as the leader and whether leading was a conscious choice.
Reflects on whether they enjoyed leading.
Identifies what they could have done differently.

items: at the beginning of your leadership journey, with clear aspirations but limited experience
keen to develop your existing leadership skills and understanding further

blocks.text: A key skill you will need to demonstrate is managing your time effectively. If you work full time or balance study with responsibilities such as childcare, you may have only a little spare time.
To gain the most benefit, set aside a certain number of hours each week for the course and any extra work. A useful place to start is identifying how you currently spend your time.

blocks.text: Time management is also a crucial skill for a leader with competing priorities. Pressure to complete a project or deliver an outcome in a short time frame can come from many sources, including senior leaders, clients, funding bodies or even governments.
Managing your time effectively can make meeting key deadlines much easier - for your studies now, and as a leader later.

pages.title: Week 2: What kind of leader could you be?

blocks.text: Last week you were introduced to the broad concepts of leadership and followership, reflected on your reasons for choosing the course and started to identify a base for developing further.

This week you'll look more closely at different leadership theories and styles, and how the context in which you lead can affect your approach. Awareness of different styles gives you a theoretical base for your own choices about the way you lead.

blocks.title: Introduction to Week 2
blocks.note: Lynne Johnson introduces the week: you'll look at leadership styles with case studies, think about what your own style may be, look at the changing face of leadership through the ages and whether there are generational or cultural differences, and explore some more recently defined leadership styles, ending with a quick quiz.

blocks.text: By the end of this week, you will be able to:

items: recognise how context can impact on leadership
identify a variety of leadership styles/approaches
assess your own leadership style

blocks.text: For decades, philosophers, researchers and business experts across the globe have tried to define effective leadership and identify a formula for leadership success. There are too many theories to cover here, so this is an overview of the most commonly discussed categories, in the order in which they were developed.

blocks.alt: Statue of the Roman Emperor Constantine, seated and holding a sword
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Leaders throughout history have had different styles and characteristics

blocks.text: **Trait theories** suggest there is a set of personal characteristics that exemplify the ideal leader.
blocks.title: Trait theories

blocks.text: Early, so-called 'great man' theories supposed that leaders are born, not made, and that these characteristics are fixed. Attitudes have changed since early trait research, but there has been renewed interest in leadership traits, for example recent studies of the emotional intelligence of leaders.
*Further reading:* Mann (1959); Stogdill (1974); Lord, DeVader and Alliger (1986); Caruso et al. (2002).

**Behavioural theories** focus on leadership as a behavioural pattern, i.e. what leaders do and how they do it. These behaviours can be learned and developed, so anyone has the potential to become a leader.
blocks.title: Behavioural theories

blocks.text: Tools have been developed to investigate leadership behaviours, such as the Leader Behaviour Description Questionnaire from Ohio State University in the 1950s and 60s. *Further reading:* Stogdill (1963); Likert (1961, 1967); Blake and Mouton (1985).
**Contingency theories** propose that effective leadership is contingent (dependent) on the situation, and that good leaders adapt their approach or style to different situations.
blocks.title: Contingency theories

blocks.text: *Further reading:* Fiedler (1964); Hersey and Blanchard (1993).

pages.title: What makes a good leader, in theory?

blocks.text: Taking these three categories together, a good leader is someone who:

items: demonstrates the right traits and skills, e.g. integrity, empathy
exhibits appropriate behaviours
adapts to the situation in which they are leading

blocks.text: The rest of the course explores these characteristics and where leadership theory goes next. What do you think is the core element of good leadership? Which theory do you identify with most?

blocks.q: Which category of theory assumes leaders are 'born, not made'?
blocks.explain: Early 'great man' trait theories saw leadership characteristics as innate and fixed. Behavioural theories assume behaviours can be learned.

blocks.title: Activity 1 Choose a theory
blocks.prompt: Choose one category - trait, behavioural or contingency theories - and research it in more detail (e.g. using the further reading suggested, or your own online or library research). Outline your findings in no more than 200 words. Then reflect: what do you think are the pros and cons of that approach to leadership?
blocks.model: While a particular theory may be discredited over time, or contradicted by other academics, there are often elements that strike a chord and lead to further research and development of its ideas. You may have your own ideas about how current theories could be developed further; leadership training opportunities are covered in Week 8.
points: Correctly summarises the chosen theory (traits, behaviours, or adapting to the situation).
Refers to some research or authors associated with the theory.
Identifies at least one strength of the approach.
Identifies at least one weakness or criticism of the approach.
blocks.hint: Allow about 30 minutes. If you feel inspired, repeat it for each theory!

blocks.text: Professor Jean Hartley, Professor of Public Leadership at The Open University, explains why a theoretical overview is useful to underpin practical experience.

blocks.title: Why leaders need theory
blocks.note: Jean Hartley: practical experience is really useful, but without theory and concepts you will struggle to understand what is going on in a situation, how you are behaving and how others react to you. Don't apply theory rigidly; draw on it. It is 'like having a deck of cards in your hand': is this a situation for a single heroic leader or for shared and distributed leadership? Does it call for transformational leadership (raising followers' energy and commitment) or transactional leadership (making sure tasks are done and purposes are clear)? Ideas about different types of follower also help you engage people, understand difficult team members and why they may feel angry, disengaged or overburdened.

blocks.text: Hartley talks about changing your style depending on the situation - which brings us to the role of context.

blocks.alt: A single pink umbrella stands out among a sea of white umbrellas
blocks.caption: Figure 2 Adapting to your context

blocks.text: Adapting your leadership to your situation is an important aspect of effective leadership, and context plays a key part in determining that situation.

Context can be drawn from international, national, local and internal perspectives, and is influenced by politics, community values and organisational culture. Two areas of particular interest are **cross-cultural** and **generational** context.
Leaders increasingly lead multicultural teams, sometimes spread across the world, and different cultures take different approaches to leadership. Interviews by House et al. (1997) highlight that:

items: the Dutch place emphasis on egalitarianism and are sceptical about the value of leadership
Iranians seek power and strength in their leaders
the Malaysian leader is expected to behave in a manner that is humble, modest and dignified
the French appreciate two kinds of leaders: a strong charismatic leader, or a consensus builder, coalition former and effective negotiator
Americans seek empowerment from leaders who grant autonomy and delegate authority, and also respect the bold, forceful, confident, risk-taking leader

blocks.text: Dempsey (2019) refers to the importance of hierarchy and dominant leadership in Latin American and Asian cultures, which can lead to tensions between colleagues with contrasting cultural viewpoints.

He also reports that approaches to staff motivation change with culture, from a focus on risk-aversion in Northeast Asia and the Middle East to a more flexible and opportunistic stance in the UK and US.
In a multicultural team, it helps if a leader is aware of potential cultural sensitivities.

blocks.q: According to House et al. (1997), which culture expects its leaders to be humble, modest and dignified?
blocks.explain: Malaysian leaders are expected to be humble, modest and dignified; the Dutch are sceptical of leadership; Iranians seek power and strength.

blocks.text: Up to five generations may be working together today. While there will always be outliers, each generation is broadly accepted to have characteristics worth knowing in cross-generational teams (summarised from the Indeed editorial team, 2022):

head: Generation
Born
Perceived characteristics
rows: Value clear hierarchies and top-down management; loyal, exert extra effort to help others; quite formal, even with peers
Favour flatter, democratic structures; value equal opportunities and friendly workplaces; measure success through personal goals; challenge processes and generate change
Entrepreneurial; value flexibility, independence, efficiency and innovation; work well with mentors; prioritise work-life balance
1981 to late 1990s (one of the largest portions of the workforce)
Technologically aware; value collaboration and open communication; motivated by meaningful work; development matters more than company loyalty
Competitive multitaskers; value technology at work; security is important; prefer flexible working; prioritise results over effort

blocks.text: These different characteristics and perceptions can bring challenges, particularly if the leader has different values from their workforce!
The key to navigating generational differences is for the leader to set aside any personal frustration, view diverse perspectives positively and be open to learning from them.

blocks.q: Which generation is described as motivated by meaningful work, valuing professional and personal development more than company loyalty?
blocks.explain: Millennials are perceived as technologically aware, collaborative and motivated by meaningful work and development.

blocks.title: Activity 2 Influences on leadership context
blocks.prompt: Choose an organisation you are part of, or would like to be part of. As its leader, list the issues you would have to consider under each heading: international trends and issues (e.g. globalisation); national trends (e.g. political policies); local influences (e.g. the role of local communities); internal influences (e.g. the culture of the organisation); cross-cultural influences (e.g. a variety of nationalities in the workforce); generational influences (e.g. a variety of generational viewpoints in the workforce).
blocks.model: Depending on your example, you may not have issues in every category, but the point is that all organisations and leaders are subject to a range of influences. You may also have thought of funding issues, attitude to risk, team motivation and so on.
points: Names a specific organisation.
Identifies international and national influences such as globalisation or government policy.
Identifies local and internal influences such as community and organisational culture.
Considers cross-cultural and generational differences in the workforce.
Recognises other influences such as funding, risk or motivation.

blocks.text: Leadership style is a sub-section of leadership theory that concentrates on the traits and behaviours of leaders. Your **leadership style** is the way in which you utilise your personality traits, learned behaviours and experience to maximise the performance of your team.

blocks.alt: Several people interacting in an open-plan office, laughing and talking; one person stands while the others sit at their desks
blocks.caption: Figure 3 Leaders have different styles

blocks.text: Many leaders benefit from frameworks, theories and definitions to guide their actions. Two leadership style frameworks follow.
The work of Kurt Lewin and colleagues in the 1930s defined three styles of leadership that are still referred to regularly today:

items: **Autocratic** - the leader makes decisions themselves, without consulting others.
**Democratic** - the leader involves followers in the decision-making process.
**Laissez faire** - the leader has little involvement, allowing followers to make their own decisions.

blocks.text: *Further reading:* Lewin (1939).

Path-Goal Theory is concerned with how leaders motivate followers to achieve specified goals. Developed by Robert House in 1971 and later updated, it incorporates leadership style, follower needs and situation, and defines four leadership behaviours:

items: **Directive** - being clear and specific about expectations, tasks and deadlines
**Supportive** - focusing on followers' needs and welfare, creating a positive working environment
**Participative** - involving followers in decision making and encouraging their ideas
**Achievement-orientated** - having high expectations and setting challenging goals you are confident followers can achieve

blocks.text: Leaders match a behaviour to the task and situation, factoring in follower characteristics such as desire for control and preference for structure. *Further reading:* House (1974); House (1996).
Such frameworks give you choices and guidance about how to lead in particular situations. This short video explains when you might use different styles.

blocks.title: Leadership styles: when to use them
blocks.note: A short external (YouTube) video explaining when you might use different leadership styles, such as Lewin's autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire styles. It refers at the end to an accompanying MindTools article on leadership styles.

blocks.q: When might you use Kurt Lewin's autocratic style of leadership?
options: When the team consists of new staff with little or no experience of a time critical task
When the team are highly motivated and knowledgeable
When a complex task needs to be carefully planned
blocks.explain: Autocratic leadership can be appropriate with a new, inexperienced team who need support to deliver a project quickly, or in a military situation with clear and present dangers.

blocks.q: When might you use Kurt Lewin's laissez faire style of leadership?
options: When the leader doesn't really know what to do
When staff are highly motivated and take pride in their work
When a task requires effective collaboration between different staff members
blocks.explain: Laissez faire is criticised as too 'hands off', but can develop and encourage motivated, capable staff with a drive to succeed. Leadership skill lies in judging which approach to adopt.

blocks.title: Match each description to the style or behaviour

pairs.def: The leader makes decisions themselves, without consulting others
The leader involves followers in the decision-making process
The leader has little involvement, letting followers make their own decisions
Being clear and specific about expectations, tasks and deadlines
Focusing on followers' needs and welfare to create a positive working environment
Involving followers in decision making and encouraging their ideas
Setting high expectations and challenging goals followers can achieve

blocks.text: Some researchers focus on a single style. Transformational and transactional leadership are regularly discussed together; transformational theories are often thought of as the next category in the evolution of leadership theory, after trait, behavioural and contingency theories.

blocks.alt: Close-up of a camera lens
blocks.caption: Figure 4 Looking through the lens at leadership styles

blocks.text: As first contrasted by James McGregor Burns (1978), **transactional** leadership focuses simply on the link between performance and reward, whereas **transformational** leadership builds a connection with followers that motivates and inspires them to achieve more.

Transactional leadership plays an important role in many organisations, particularly where there is a focus on standards and procedures. Transactional leaders are process and action oriented and are particularly effective when projects must be tightly controlled, e.g. on a production line with low paid employees. Their responsive, directive style can be useful in emergencies.

items: **Advantage:** clarity - employees know what's expected and have incentives to perform well.
**Disadvantage:** lack of autonomy, potentially demotivating both leader and employees.

blocks.text: Bill Gates is often given as an example, particularly in his early days at Microsoft when reward and punishment were a key focus. Many commentators also view Steve Jobs, former CEO of Apple, as transactional, famous for his strong focus on tasks and structures.
Transformational leadership has become one of the most popular leadership concepts. Bass (1985) developed it further, defining four basic elements, the four 'I's:

items: **Individualised consideration** - supporting individual followers; coaching and developing them
**Intellectual stimulation** - encouraging followers to solve problems creatively for themselves
**Inspirational motivation** - inspiring and enthusing followers through clear communication of the vision
**Idealised influence (charisma)** - being a role model; having high moral and ethical standards

blocks.alt: A South African bank note featuring Nelson Mandela, surrounded by coins
blocks.caption: Figure 5 Nelson Mandela

blocks.text: A well-known case study (Penn State blog, 2013) of transformational leadership is Nelson Mandela, the first black President of South Africa. He motivated and inspired his followers to end apartheid by encouraging them to come up with their own solutions (*intellectual stimulation*), showing personal concern for the struggles of individual followers (*individualised consideration*), and repeatedly articulating a clear vision with charisma and conviction.

blocks.title: Match each example to one of Bass's four 'I's

pairs.def: Coaching a team member and showing concern for their personal struggles
Encouraging followers to come up with their own creative solutions
Enthusing followers by clearly and repeatedly communicating the vision
Acting as a role model with high moral and ethical standards

pages.title: Activity 4 What makes a transformational leader?

blocks.title: Activity 4 What makes a transformational leader?
blocks.prompt: Think of someone you consider to be a transformational leader - someone you work with, a community leader or a historical figure. Present three pieces of evidence that demonstrate their transformational style.
blocks.model: For example, Walt Disney, animator and founder of one of the top motion picture companies, is often quoted as a transformational leader: (1) he had a very clear vision of what he wanted to achieve and understood he couldn't do it alone; (2) he was charismatic, with infectious, motivating enthusiasm; (3) he was creative, encouraging his team to explore new ideas and offering personal support when needed.
points: Names a specific leader.
Gives evidence of a clear, well-communicated vision (inspirational motivation).
Gives evidence of charisma or acting as a role model (idealised influence).
Gives evidence of encouraging creativity or supporting individuals (intellectual stimulation, individualised consideration).
blocks.hint: Allow about 10 minutes. Use the four 'I's as a checklist.

blocks.text: Although transformational leadership is mainly viewed positively, it has potential negatives:

items: Transformational leaders often struggle with detail; carried away by passion and enthusiasm, they may miss what the facts are telling them and lead the organisation in the wrong direction.
Their approach may not meet all followers' needs, so they can end up working closely with a small cohort and isolating other team members.
Their enthusiasm might lead them to expect too much from followers, such as working long hours.

blocks.q: Transactional leadership's key advantage is that employees know what is expected of them and have incentives to perform well.
blocks.explain: Clarity is the key advantage; the main disadvantage is lack of autonomy, which can demotivate leader and employees.

blocks.text: Historically, leadership research focused on male leaders, often in large private-sector organisations in North America. Today's research considers the perspectives of male and female followers, peers and supervisors from a diverse range of organisations and countries, and this has led to more inclusive leadership styles.

blocks.alt: A telescope on a tripod stand
blocks.caption: Figure 6 A focus on leadership styles

blocks.text: Simply stated, adaptive leaders prepare and encourage people to deal with change.

Adaptive leadership helps people and organisations adapt to changing and challenging environments. It was developed by Ronald Heifetz with colleagues during the 1990s and beyond. He explains that 'adaptive work is required when our deeply held beliefs are challenged, when the values that made us successful become less relevant, and when legitimate yet competing perspectives emerge' (Heifetz and Laurie, 1997).
Heifetz and Laurie define six leader behaviours key to the process:

items: *Get on the balcony* - step back from the 'field of action' and look from a different perspective
*Identify the adaptive challenge* - find out what the key challenge is
*Regulate distress* - manage conflict and provide direction for your followers
*Maintain disciplined attention* - encourage followers to remain open to, and learn from, conflicting points of view
*Give the work back to the people* - empower followers to solve their own problems
*Protect voices of leadership from below* - encourage junior staff to share their concerns and don't dismiss them

blocks.text: Heifetz separates adaptive from technical challenges:

head: Technical challenges
Adaptive challenges
rows: Solved through the leader's authority and/or expertise
Require a range of expertise and a supportive, collaborative environment

blocks.q: A team must change long-held working habits after new regulations arrive, and nobody is sure what the full problem is. What kind of challenge is this in Heifetz's terms?
options: Technical - the leader's expertise can solve it
Adaptive - it is not clearly defined and needs collaboration
Neither - it is a management issue only
blocks.explain: Adaptive challenges are not clearly defined and need a range of expertise and a supportive, collaborative environment; technical ones can be solved by the leader's authority or expertise.

pages.title: Activity 5 What are your adaptive challenges?

blocks.title: Activity 5 What are your adaptive challenges?
blocks.prompt: Consider an adaptive challenge you have faced at work or in your personal life (e.g. implementing new regulations at work, or changing your lifestyle to correct a health issue). What was the challenge? What was difficult about adapting? What personal behaviours or habits did you have to change? What specific actions did you take? Who else needed to be involved to ensure success, and what was their approach?
blocks.model: Change can be difficult and distressing for many people, and an effective leader will address that, even while adapting their own behaviours and values. Was your example difficult or distressing? Did you receive support from a leader? Understanding theories like this one, and having a list such as Heifetz and Laurie's six behaviours to refer to, can help you lead change in a difficult environment. Leading change is covered in Week 6.
points: Describes a specific challenge that required adapting beliefs, habits or behaviour.
Explains what made adapting difficult or distressing.
Identifies the behaviours changed and actions taken.
Recognises who else was involved and how they supported the change.

blocks.text: Goniewicz and Hertelendy (2023) argue that 'in the post-pandemic world, adaptive leadership becomes even more vital as it requires strategic foresight, empathy, resilience, and effective communication.' Drawing on lessons from COVID-19, they recommend that leaders:

items: adopt a learning mindset, both personally and organisationally
prioritise mental health and wellbeing, investing resources to help teams manage stress and keep a healthy work-life balance
forge partnerships with other organisations, sectors and countries to share knowledge, resources and best practice
address systemic inequalities, creating inclusive, equitable environments to ensure future resilience
enhance crisis management skills such as rapid decision making and effective resource allocation

blocks.text: 'Creating inclusive, equitable environments' is increasingly important in any leadership situation as the workforce grows more diverse and global collaboration expands. A report for the Employer Network for Equality and Inclusion (ENEI, 2016), based on a survey of almost 1000 employees and 61 interviews in 11 organisations, defines an inclusive leader as an 'exemplar of inclusive behaviour' who:

items: listens to and seeks out the views of diverse people and takes account of them, without bias, in decisions
appreciates that a diverse group will generate more creative solutions, and encourages this
inspires people through a shared vision of future success and motivates them to deliver it
leverages difference for high performance and responsive excellence to customers', clients' and service users' needs
provides positive feedback to boost people's self-efficacy
helps diverse people identify and develop their talents for performance now and future advancement
communicates authentically and honestly in a way that inspires trust, loyalty and well-being

blocks.text: The ENEI report also describes 15 core competencies of an inclusive leader, ranging from empathy and confidence building to stewardship and healing. You'll explore a selection of leadership skills in Week 3; OpenLearn's course *Diversity and inclusion in the workplace* is a useful resource if you want to go further.

Inclusive leadership has not yet been extensively researched, but there is evidence of benefits ranging from the promotion of psychological safety and work engagement (Nembhard and Edmondson, 2006) to innovative work behaviour (Qi, Liu, Wei and Hu, 2019).

blocks.q: Which of these are behaviours of an inclusive leader according to ENEI (2016)? Select all that apply.
options: Seeks out diverse views and takes account of them without bias
Makes decisions alone to avoid conflict
Provides positive feedback to boost self-efficacy
Helps diverse people identify and develop their talents
blocks.explain: Inclusive leaders listen to diverse views without bias, boost self-efficacy with positive feedback and develop people's talents; deciding alone is the opposite of inclusion.

blocks.alt: Office building with the Deloitte sign
blocks.caption: Figure 7 Deloitte

blocks.text: Like many global firms, Deloitte offers pro bono programmes, from an annual day of service to immersive international projects, and uses them to cultivate inclusive leaders. A report (Taproot Foundation, 2021) shares six stories of US-based Deloitte professionals connecting pro bono experience to inclusive leadership traits. One trait is **curiosity**.

Robert helped a non-profit serving high-risk young people to quantify the impact of a programme. His team knew strategic communications and data analysis but not the client's intervention model. 'Robert saw first-hand how powerful curiosity can be. He learned to ask open-ended questions and facilitate conversations that brought together the Deloitte team's expertise and the client's knowledge.'

pages.title: An inclusive environment is a curious one

blocks.text: An inclusive environment must also be a curious one. Inclusive leaders constantly ask questions, recognising that knowledge from others can fill in the gaps in the bigger picture. They create an environment of inquiry to discover where new passions may lie. This openness can create a space for teams to safely push and inspire each other to the highest quality results.

blocks.q: Inclusive leadership has already been extensively researched, with conclusive results.
blocks.explain: It has not yet been extensively researched, although evidence suggests benefits such as psychological safety, work engagement and innovative work behaviour.

pages.title: Try it: lead in different situations

blocks.title: Try it: situational leadership simulator
blocks.intro: Contingency theories say good leaders adapt their style to the situation. Lead nine different teams - from new temps to senior experts, a merger and a global team - and choose the style or behaviour that fits, using Lewin, Path-Goal, transactional/transformational, adaptive and inclusive leadership.

blocks.text: Are you an autocratic leader, or do you prefer the transformational style? Are you facing significant change in your organisation and feeling drawn to the adaptive approach?

blocks.alt: A row of white business shirts hanging on a rail
blocks.caption: Figure 8 What is your leadership style?

blocks.text: There are no right or wrong answers. Many experts conclude that your leadership style is not fixed, and that you can adapt and develop it as your career progresses.

blocks.title: Activity 6 How do you lead?
blocks.prompt: Write three words that you feel describe your leadership style. If you need inspiration: if someone were observing you in a leadership role, what would you want them to see, hear and feel?
blocks.model: Are you happy with your current style? Would an observer see different elements to the ones you outlined? Would you like to make changes? Experts agree you can change your leadership style: learn different skills and behaviours, implement elements of the models here and in the wider literature, or choose a style that inspires you and work towards it.
points: Gives three words describing their leadership style.
Considers how an observer would see, hear and feel their leadership.
Reflects on whether they would like to change or develop their style.
Links their style to a model or style from this week.

blocks.text: Many online tools analyse leadership style. They don't give a definitive outcome, but reflect your preferences for different styles and approaches. Examples suggested by the course: *Skills You Need: What sort of leader are you?*, *Coach-You: Leadership style assessment*, *The Foundation of Nursing Leadership: What is your leadership style?* and *Psychologies: What's your natural leadership style?* If you use another tool, make sure it is free.

blocks.title: Activity 7 Leadership style questionnaires
blocks.prompt: Do one free online leadership style questionnaire and summarise your results: which styles or preferences did it highlight, did they surprise you, and which questions made you think about your approach to leading?
blocks.model: These questionnaires are not intended to give a definitive analysis of your style or skills, but their questions can stimulate your thoughts about your approach to leading. Keep this summary for your leadership skills audit in Week 3. For more depth, Northouse's *Leadership Theory and Practice* covers a different style in each chapter, with a questionnaire for each.
points: Names the tool used and summarises the result.
Relates the result to styles covered this week.
Reflects critically: the result is an indication of preferences, not definitive.
Notes questions or insights to use in the Week 3 skills audit.

blocks.q: Which theory proposes that good leaders adapt their approach to different situations?
blocks.explain: Contingency theories say effective leadership depends on the situation.

blocks.q: Path-Goal Theory, developed by Robert House, is mainly concerned with:
options: How leaders motivate followers to achieve specified goals
Identifying the traits leaders are born with
blocks.explain: Path-Goal Theory combines style, follower needs and situation to explain how leaders motivate followers towards goals, using four behaviours.

blocks.q: Behavioural theories assume that leadership behaviours can be learned, so anyone has the potential to become a leader.
blocks.explain: That assumption distinguishes behavioural theories from early trait theories.

blocks.q: Which of these is one of Heifetz and Laurie's six adaptive leader behaviours?
blocks.explain: 'Get on the balcony' means stepping back from the field of action to see a different perspective.

blocks.q: Who first contrasted transactional and transformational leadership?
blocks.explain: Burns (1978) first contrasted them; Bass (1985) developed transformational leadership further with the four 'I's.

blocks.q: What is the key to leading teams with different generational characteristics?
options: Adopting the values of the youngest generation
Treating everyone the same and ignoring differences
Setting aside personal frustration, viewing diverse perspectives positively and learning from them
blocks.explain: The leader should set aside frustration, see diverse perspectives positively and be open to learning from them.

blocks.text: You should now feel better informed about leadership theories and styles, and more aware of the leadership literature you can access. You have explored the impact context can have on leadership, learned about key styles including transactional, transformational, adaptive and inclusive leadership, and considered your own style.
You should now feel that you can:

items: recognise how context can impact on leadership
identify a variety of leadership styles/approaches
assess your own leadership style

blocks.text: Next week you'll focus on the specific skills and behaviours required of an effective leader, from the perspectives of a range of employers, and start to look at your own leadership skills and how to develop them.

chapters.title: Week 3: What makes a good leader?
chapters.summary: The skills and behaviours employers look for in leaders, auditing and building your own skills, finding a mentor and keeping a leadership journal.

blocks.text: Last week you looked at leadership theories and styles, and how the context in which you lead affects how you lead. This week, with that theory underpinning your thinking, you'll focus on the **skills that employers look for** in successful leaders. You'll consider leadership frameworks from major employers across different sectors and reflect on your own skills using a skills audit.

blocks.title: Lynne Johnson introduces Week 3
blocks.note: Lynne points out that by now you'll have met many average leaders, a few bad ones, a few good ones and hopefully some outstanding ones. So what makes a really good leader, and what key skills and behaviours do organisations look for when choosing people for leadership roles? This week covers that, plus assessing and building your own leadership skills and keeping track of your journey.

blocks.text: By the end of this week, you will be able to:

items: recognise key skills and behaviours required for effective leadership
review your own experience and capability in using these skills
identify opportunities to build your skills and experience
use a leadership journal to reflect on your experience.

pages.title: Why employers care about leadership skills

blocks.text: The academic perspective on leadership is important, but so is the **employer's** perspective, particularly if you want a leadership role. Leadership skills matter to employers for several reasons:

items: Evidence suggests that employees with leadership skills and ambitions remain loyal to their organisation, have fewer work absences and higher morale.
Change is constant in business, and effective change requires leaders with the right skills.
Succession planning is crucial, so most employers are keen to train and develop their future leaders.
Effective leaders lead to successful businesses; ineffective leadership can lead to failure.

blocks.alt: A man stands next to a complex black and white line drawing of charts, icons and diagrams that covers an entire wall
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Leadership skills and the employer

pages.title: Activity 1: Your list of leadership skills

blocks.text: Before looking at employers' requirements, focus for a few minutes on your own view of leadership and the skills you think are important. If you considered skills when defining leadership in Week 1, Activity 1, refer back to that now.

blocks.title: Activity 1 Leadership skills list
blocks.prompt: In five minutes, list all the leadership skills you can think of.
blocks.model: It is impossible to provide a definitive list, but the most commonly described leadership skills and abilities include the competence to communicate, motivate, make decisions, solve problems and delegate, combined with self-awareness, creativity, positivity and integrity.
points: Communication and the ability to motivate others are core leadership skills.
Making decisions and solving problems are commonly listed.
Delegating is an important leadership ability.
Personal qualities such as self-awareness, creativity, positivity and integrity matter.
blocks.hint: Allow about 5 minutes. Think of leaders you admire: what do they do well?

blocks.text: Many business leaders share their experience online or in print, and their hints and tips are often worth reading. For example, Sir Richard Branson, entrepreneur and founder of the Virgin Group, values these leadership qualities and attributes (Half, 2016):

items: the ability to think differently
an eye for talent
a positive company culture
the ability to delegate
willingness to listen and learn
a hands-on approach
the ability to make decisions (and move on from mistakes)
attention to detail
passion for the job.

blocks.alt: The red and white frontage of Branson's Centre of Entrepreneurship on a city street
blocks.caption: Figure 2 Branson's Centre of Entrepreneurship

blocks.text: One of the most important elements of effective leadership, and a key theme in current discussion of leadership skills, is **emotional intelligence**.
The 'ability to monitor one's own and others' feelings and emotions, to discriminate among them and to use this information to guide one's thinking and actions.' (Mayer and Salovey, 1990, p. 189)
blocks.title: Emotional intelligence

blocks.text: Daniel Goleman (1998) adapted their model to identify five basic emotional and social competencies:

items: self-awareness
self-regulation
motivation
empathy
social skills.

blocks.text: This video from Harvard Business Review explains the value of emotional intelligence, examining each of Goleman's five competencies in turn. In Section 2 you'll see how some of these qualities are reflected in the competency frameworks used by a range of employers.

blocks.title: Daniel Goleman: what makes a leader?
blocks.note: Harvard Business Review video in which Daniel Goleman explains the value of emotional intelligence for leaders and examines each of the five competencies: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills. It also explains how emotional intelligence can be developed.

pages.title: What employers look for: the NHS

blocks.text: Employers emphasise different leadership skills depending on their context, as you can see by comparing leadership frameworks. You'll now look at five frameworks from sectors ranging from healthcare to corporate finance. Organisations tweak and update these regularly, so they were correct at the time of writing.
**1. Healthcare.** The NHS has six core principles, branded 'Our Leadership Way', focusing on the heart, head and hands of leadership (Leadership Academy, 2023):

head: Focus
Principles
rows: We are inclusive, promote equality and diversity and challenge discrimination. We are kind and treat people with compassion, courtesy and respect.
We aim for the highest standards and seek to continually improve harnessing our ingenuity. We can be trusted to do what we promise.
We collaborate, forming effective partnerships to achieve our common goals. We celebrate success and support our people to be the best they can be.

pages.title: The humanitarian sector: the UN's IASC

blocks.alt: A complex, spiralling metal framework supporting a glass roof on a building
blocks.caption: Figure 3 There are many leadership frameworks

blocks.text: **2. Humanitarian sector.** The UN's Inter-Agency Standing Committee (IASC) has agreed competencies that are critical for humanitarian coordination and leadership (Inter-Agency Standing Committee, 2021):

head: Competency
Includes
rows: Formulating strategies, applying humanitarian principles and norms; deciding and initiating action
Relating and networking; fostering humanitarian teamwork
Advocacy and negotiation; presenting and communicating information
Coping with pressure and setbacks; adapting and responding to change

blocks.text: **3. Higher education.** The University of Cambridge presents its leadership attributes framework visually, as a circle divided into four quadrants, each linked to a group of attributes.

blocks.alt: A circle divided into four coloured quadrants, each connected to a list of attributes outside the circle
blocks.caption: Figure 4 University of Cambridge's leadership attributes framework, 2020

head: Quadrant
Attributes
rows: Achieving excellence in performance in context of governance
Strategy & direction; Decision making & delivering results; Commitment
Managing in an environment of change
Financial acumen; Creativity & innovation; Risk & opportunity; Philanthropy
People development: engaging and developing others
Relationship building; Teamwork; Develop people & mentorship

blocks.text: **4. Private sector.** PwC is a professional services company providing specialist advice to businesses. One of the five attributes in its **PwC Professional** leadership development framework is 'Whole leadership', explained as:
The ability to lead yourself and others to make a difference and create a positive impact in a responsible, authentic, resilient, inclusive and passionate manner.
This is followed by three questions:

items: Can you lead yourself?
Can you lead others?
Are you purpose-led and values driven?

blocks.text: **5. Technology.** The technology sector often takes a less formal approach. For example, an in-house research project at Google identified 10 behaviour styles common to highly rated managers (Google re:Work, n.d.). A highly rated manager:

items: Is a good coach
Delegates to the team and does not micromanage
Has an inclusive approach that takes into account not only the team's performance, but also their well-being and fulfilment
Is highly productive and results-oriented
Communicates effectively: listens carefully and shares information
Supports career development and discusses performance
Has a clear vision/strategy and shares it with their team
Has the expertise to advise the team
Collaborates across departments
Is decisive.

blocks.text: Common themes across these frameworks focus on **developing people, inclusion and communication**. Other themes reflect sector priorities: influencing and representing are key across the humanitarian sector, and compassion is understandably high on the NHS agenda. Emotional intelligence also runs through many of these frameworks, supporting inclusivity, authenticity and relationships with others.

blocks.title: Match each framework feature to the employer

pairs.def: 'Our Leadership Way': heart, head and hands - compassionate, curious, collaborative
Competencies include influencing and representing, managing complexity, adapting and coping
A circle of four quadrants, e.g. personal leadership and managing in an environment of change
'Whole leadership': can you lead yourself, lead others, and are you purpose-led and values driven?
10 behaviours of highly rated managers, from being a good coach to being decisive

blocks.text: These models each emphasise different facets of leadership. Some are presented very formally, others more informally. Most are clear that the themes and dimensions should apply to **all employees**, regardless of their role.

If you are interested in working with **small to medium-sized enterprises (SMEs)**, you may have to look harder for their preferred leadership competencies. Smaller organisations often don't have the resources to develop and publicise such structures.
Talk to someone in a senior position to understand their priorities, or look for clues on the organisation's website or in its annual report.
blocks.title: Researching an SME

pages.title: Activity 2: What leadership skills do employers value?

blocks.title: Activity 2 What leadership skills do employers value?
blocks.prompt: Choose the leadership frameworks of at least two different employers - the ones outlined here, or an organisation that means something to you (look in a framework, development programme, job description or recruitment literature). Then consider: 1) What are the similarities? 2) What are the differences? 3) Are they written in a different style? 4) Do they highlight different skills? 5) Can you see why they focus on different elements based on their context? 6) Do you feel more aligned to a particular style or culture?
blocks.model: The more you understand about the ethos of leadership in an organisation, the better you'll be at aligning yourself with its culture and progressing within it. If you looked at your own or a target organisation, you now have a list of skills to develop - or you may realise its ethos doesn't suit you. Comparing two frameworks shows the relevance of context again, and reflecting that understanding is attractive to employers when you apply.
points: Understanding an organisation's leadership ethos helps you align with its culture and progress.
The frameworks reveal skills you may need to develop.
You might find an organisation's ethos does not suit you.
Differences between frameworks reflect each organisation's context.
Showing you understand an employer's context is attractive in applications.

pages.title: Video: Key skills employers look for

blocks.title: Rebecca Fielding: key skills and attributes in leaders
blocks.note: Rebecca Fielding, drawing on her experience recruiting leaders, says there is no 'secret sauce': different organisations look for different things, and the most important thing is to be the authentic, best version of yourself. Whatever label employers use (values, behaviours, competencies, strengths), she sees common qualities: self-awareness and striving for improvement; self-belief, because there is no handbook telling you if a decision is right; good decision-making, using your intellect to make the best decision you can with often imperfect information; and communication skills - great leaders spend much more time explaining why, not just what.

blocks.text: Rebecca's qualities range from self-awareness and self-belief to making good decisions and communicating effectively with your team. You'll explore these in more detail later in the course.

Understanding the skills employers value is essential preparation for a leadership role: they will look for **evidence** that you have them. Next, you'll assess your own skills and identify gaps in your experience.

A **skills audit** is a useful way to review your skills and gauge how well developed you think they are. It can help to refer to a recent CV or application form, as this will remind you of what you've already done.

blocks.alt: A dial labelled 'Skill level' with a red needle that can point to low, moderate, high or maximum; it points to maximum
blocks.caption: Figure 5 A skills audit is a useful way to review your skills

blocks.text: In the next activity, score your level of expertise against each skill like this:

These skills commonly appear in leadership job descriptions: inspiring and motivating others; creating and sharing a clear vision; empathy; integrity; diplomacy; resilience; initiative; self-awareness; self-reflection; self-motivation; influencing others; relationship building; negotiation; team working; verbal communication; listening; presentation skills; driving/leading change; problem solving; decision making; taking risks; multitasking; planning and organising; strategic thinking; financial acumen; evaluating information; analytical thinking.

blocks.title: Activity 3 Personal skills audit
blocks.prompt: Score yourself 0-3 (0 = no experience yet, 1 = basic, 2 = competent, 3 = proficient) against each skill listed above, adding any of your own from job descriptions or experience. Give at least one example of when you've demonstrated each skill. Then summarise your strengths and areas for development - and ask a colleague, manager, mentor or friend who knows you well whether they agree.
blocks.model: Group your skills by score (all the 3s, all the 2s, etc.) to see your perceived strengths and areas for development. Is there an obvious gap in your experience, or is your next step to grow your overall expertise from basic to competent? Talking to someone who knows you well helps you check whether your self-perceptions are accurate, and they may have ideas to add. Many people underestimate their own abilities.
points: Grouping skills by score shows your strengths and areas for development.
Look for obvious gaps or a general need to move from basic to competent.
Give concrete evidence for each skill.
Ask someone who knows you well to check your self-assessment.
Many people underestimate their own abilities.
blocks.hint: Allow about 30 minutes. Keep a recent CV or application form to hand.

blocks.text: In a leadership role, your employer will also assess your skills, for example through a performance review or appraisal. If you can, use feedback from those assessments to enhance your audit.

blocks.title: Rebecca Fielding: how leaders are assessed
blocks.note: Rebecca explains the most common method, the annual appraisal or performance review (sometimes with a mid-year review) with your line manager. It looks at what you delivered against your KPIs (Key Performance Indicators) and objectives, and how you delivered it - the organisation's values, behaviours and competencies - often ending in a grade or rating. Other methods: psychometrics, which test how you think and perform as a leader through scenarios; 360-degree feedback from clients, team, boss and peers; and development centres, like in-house assessment centres with group, role-play and written exercises. Most simply, managers and colleagues observe you every day and give feedback.

items: Appraisal / performance review
Psychometric tests
360-degree feedback
Development centres
Everyday observation and feedback

blocks.text: In Week 1, Activity 4, you reflected on your leadership experience so far. Wherever you are on the spectrum, there is always more to learn. Opportunities in and outside work include:

items: **Joining a club or society:** a committee role such as treasurer, chair or social secretary gives useful leadership experience.
**Leading a local community project or campaign:** helps develop a wide range of skills, particularly interacting with people.
**Organising a fundraising event or social gathering:** needs extensive skills, from decision making and planning to relationship building and negotiating.
**Mentoring or coaching someone:** focuses on a crucial element of leadership - listening to people and helping them develop.

blocks.alt: A group of people picking up litter
blocks.caption: Figure 6 Voluntary work is a great way to build up leadership skills

blocks.title: Activity 4 Developing your skills
blocks.prompt: Look at the strengths and areas for development from Activity 3 and prioritise those most relevant now (you don't need every skill, especially early in your leadership journey). Note ideas for projects or activities that would help, e.g. chair a working group, volunteer to give a presentation, organise an event. Ask yourself: Do I need to focus on a key area, such as interpersonal skills or negotiating experience? Which projects could build those skills, e.g. fundraising for a local charity, or changing my approach with a member of staff I struggle to connect with?
blocks.model: Involving your mentor, manager or another leader who knows you will be useful: they may suggest options you hadn't considered or weren't aware of. For more detail, try the GROW framework - Goal, Reality, Options, What will you do next? - to plan your actions.
points: Prioritise the development areas most relevant to you now.
Identify concrete projects or activities that build those skills.
Involve a mentor, manager or experienced leader for ideas.
The GROW model (Goal, Reality, Options, What next) can structure your plan.

blocks.text: A leadership **mentor or coach** in your organisation can guide you towards useful experiences and may put your name forward. Ask Human Resources whether your employer runs leadership development schemes. If not, identify a leader you'd like to be like and approach them for advice. Outside your organisation, or if you're not in work, join a relevant LinkedIn or other social network group and look for someone with interesting things to say about leadership.
Top tips for finding a mentor

items: It must be someone with more experience than you.
Rapport is easier if you choose someone you respect and who shares your values.
The relationship must be honest, so choose someone you trust to keep conversations confidential.
Consider people inside and outside your organisation, e.g. someone you met at a conference or networking event.

blocks.title: Activity 5 Finding a mentor
blocks.prompt: Part 1: List individuals, in your organisation or elsewhere, whom you could approach for leadership advice or mentoring. Part 2: Prepare some key questions to ask them, for example: What are the key skills a good leader needs? What do you wish you had known before your first leadership role? Can you describe your path to leadership?
blocks.model: Before requesting a formal mentoring relationship, you might arrange an informal first meeting to ask some questions and see whether you could work together; either way you'll gain insights. You could ask how they would find a mentor. If you don't feel ready for a mentor yet, talk to everyone on your list, ask your questions and add them to your network of contacts.
points: Name specific people inside or outside your organisation.
Prepare focused questions about skills, experience and paths to leadership.
An informal first meeting helps you judge whether you could work together.
Even without a formal mentor, these conversations build your network.
blocks.hint: Allow about 20 minutes. The OpenLearn course 'Exploring career mentoring and coaching' covers this in more detail.

blocks.text: Most leaders have complex, challenging jobs, so it can be hard to make time to reflect. Writing a **journal** helps you clarify and explore thoughts, questions and concerns in a way that can't happen while they compete for attention in your head. It's an excellent habit to start early. You can use it to:

items: capture and explore ideas, or note questions you'd like to answer
look back on events: how you felt, what you did and what you could do differently
rehearse future conversations that might be difficult
facilitate decision making: clarify the decision and explore pros and cons
note anything of interest: quotes, goals, feelings, lessons learned
note things that went well - **positive reinforcement**, which can boost confidence in difficult times.

blocks.alt: A colourful pile of notebooks and an electronic tablet on a wooden table
blocks.caption: Figure 7 A leadership journal is an important tool

blocks.text: Over time, reflect on what you've written and look for patterns or themes that give insight into your typical behaviours and responses.

blocks.title: Activity 6 Starting your journal
blocks.prompt: Choose an online journal/app or a notebook and pen, and the best time of day to write with no distractions. Set aside 15 minutes to write about what's currently in your head, focusing on your leadership interests and the aims for this course you set in Week 1, Activity 5. Ask yourself questions, jot down ideas, revisit recent events, or outline goals (e.g. 'What would I do if I had an extra hour every day?' or 'How would I like to describe myself as a leader?'). Write your first entry, then reflect: how could this help you become a better leader?
blocks.model: Reflection is a skill: it can feel difficult or awkward at first, but it gets easier with practice. The key is to make the time. If every day seems too much, set aside 10-15 minutes each week to start with, and schedule a slot in your diary if you journal at work.
points: Reflection is a skill that improves with practice.
The key is making regular time for it.
Start small, e.g. 10-15 minutes a week, and schedule it.
Journaling helps you clarify thinking and learn from experience.

blocks.text: Models such as **Gibbs' (1988) reflective cycle** can give structure to your reflection. It focuses on what you were thinking and feeling, what was good and bad about the experience and what sense you can make of it, before considering what could have been done differently and what you'd do if it happened again.

blocks.alt: Six boxes in a clockwise cycle: Description, Feelings, Evaluation, Analysis, Conclusion, Action plan
blocks.caption: Figure 8 Gibbs' reflective cycle

items: **Description** - What happened?
**Feelings** - What were you thinking/feeling?
**Evaluation** - What was good/bad about the experience?
**Analysis** - What sense can you make of the situation?
**Conclusion** - What else could you have done?
**Action plan** - If it arose again, what would you do?

blocks.q: Who defined emotional intelligence as the 'ability to monitor one's own and others' feelings and emotions… and to use this information to guide one's thinking and actions'?
blocks.explain: The definition comes from Mayer and Salovey (1990); Goleman later adapted their model into five competencies.

blocks.q: Which of these are among Goleman's five emotional and social competencies? Select all that apply.
blocks.explain: Goleman's five are self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills.

blocks.q: In the NHS 'Our Leadership Way', which value is linked to the 'heart'?
blocks.explain: Heart = Compassionate, Head = Curious, Hands = Collaborative.

blocks.q: Small and medium-sized enterprises usually publish detailed leadership competency frameworks.
blocks.explain: SMEs often lack the resources to develop and publicise such frameworks, so you may need to talk to senior staff or look at their website or annual report.

blocks.q: What is 360-degree feedback?
options: A yearly review with your line manager only
Feedback from clients, team, boss, peers and others around you
A written exercise at a development centre
blocks.explain: It gathers feedback from everyone around you - hence '360 degrees'.

blocks.q: In Gibbs' reflective cycle, which stage asks 'What sense can you make of the situation?'
blocks.explain: Analysis follows Evaluation and comes before Conclusion ('What else could you have done?').

blocks.text: You've looked at the leadership skills employers value, audited which you already have and identified those to gain or enhance. You've explored opportunities for leadership development, recognised the benefits of mentors and reflective practice, thought about people who could advise and support you, and taken the first steps in building your leadership journal.
You should now feel that you can:

items: recognise key skills and behaviours required for effective leadership
review your own experience and capability in using these skills
identify opportunities to build your skills and experience
use a leadership journal to reflect on your experience.

blocks.text: Next week, you'll look at the impact of bad leadership: the common mistakes leaders make and ways to rectify them. Learning from the mistakes of others can be a very valuable leadership experience.

chapters.title: Week 4: When leadership goes wrong
chapters.summary: Recognising ineffective and destructive leadership, its impact on followers and organisations, common leadership mistakes and the skills that help put them right.
