blocks.text: Last week you looked at leadership skills: why employers value them and how you can develop yours. This week you move your focus from good leadership to **bad**. You'll consider the spectrum of poor leadership and the common mistakes leaders make. Learning from those mistakes might help you avoid making them yourself.

blocks.title: Lynne Johnson introduces Week 4
blocks.note: Lynne notes that to do things right we often have to make mistakes and learn from them, but we can also learn from what happens around us. Have you ever seen or experienced really poor leadership? This week looks at the common mistakes leaders make, defines destructive leadership, explores the impact of bad or weak leadership on a team and, importantly, how to turn it around.

blocks.text: By the end of this week, you will be able to:

items: recognise poor leadership in different forms
reflect on the impact of poor or weak leadership
describe ways in which leadership mistakes might be avoided.

blocks.text: Poor leadership can be described on a **spectrum**. This course concentrates on the poor leadership you're likely to meet in the workplace, ranging from the common mistakes many leaders make to leaders who are 'destructive'.

blocks.alt: A shiny black business shoe crushing several egg shells with worried faces drawn on them
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Poor leadership can damage your team

blocks.text: At some point a leader in your organisation, or in public life, will have made a decision you disagree with, or upset people with a damaging comment. Some show negative behaviours over a long period, harming morale. Have you ever wondered why? Was it pressure, their circumstances, or a lack of the skills to handle the situation?

pages.title: Activity 1: Your experience of poor leadership

blocks.title: Activity 1 Your experience of poor or weak leadership
blocks.prompt: Part 1: Think of a time when you felt shocked, offended, disappointed or angry at an action taken by a leader you follow. Briefly summarise the situation and how you felt. What made it poor leadership? Part 2: Now put yourself in the leader's position. What could you have done differently?
blocks.model: When you considered what you would do differently, what were the key differences? Would you use different skills, different language or a different method of communication? Would you seek out and apply knowledge the leader didn't have and should have asked for? Reflecting on how a situation could have been handled more effectively is important for any leader, and your leadership journal is a useful tool for it.
points: Describe the situation and why it felt like poor leadership.
Consider different skills, language or ways of communicating.
Think about information the leader lacked and should have sought.
Reflecting on how a situation could be handled better is a key leadership habit.

pages.title: When the poor leader is you

blocks.text: Sometimes the poor or weak leader might be **you**. Have you ever had feedback that surprised you, or coaching that encouraged you to reflect on your own actions? Professor Jean Hartley explains the importance of reviewing yourself.

blocks.title: Jean Hartley: reviewing your own leadership
blocks.note: Jean Hartley says it can be hard to review your own leadership, but continual low-key self-monitoring is important. Your environment gives you data: others' body language, meeting dynamics that feel wrong (long pauses, reluctance to speak, only the most powerful speaking), an angry clash, or 'active passivity' - everyone agrees what should be done but it doesn't get done. Ask what your purpose as a leader is and how far you achieve it. Many experienced leaders reflect critically on the journey home or keep a reflective journal. You can also draw in others: a mentor, a coach or an action learning set.

blocks.text: Many things can affect your leadership, from being forced to lead on a vision you don't share, to a lack of confidence in your skills and a feeling of being out of your depth. Sometimes you might just have a bad day!

Many leaders find **coaching and reflection** invaluable for reviewing their actions. This week helps you recognise the wrong behaviours and consider more successful alternatives. Use the leadership journal you started in Week 3 to identify where you might be going wrong and how to improve.

blocks.title: Jean Hartley: if your leadership isn't working
blocks.note: Jean advises first analysing the situation to work out what help would be useful. If someone gets under your skin and you're more irritable with them, take it to your coach and find a different way of working with them. If you lack technical skill or understanding of your team, read up or spend more time with team members. If you can't put your finger on what isn't working, talk to a trusted friend who listens and questions well, a mentor, or read around the subject - you may need to try more than one thing. Many things take months or years to improve: 'fall down seven times, get up eight'. Nobody's perfect; be kind to yourself.

blocks.text: There is growing academic interest in the negative side of leadership. Schyns and Schilling (2013) give two main reasons:

items: the prevalence of destructive leader behaviours in organisations, and the associated costs
findings that the effects of destructive leaders on their followers are severe.

blocks.alt: Lego mini figures of Darth Vader and a Stormtrooper facing each other against a red background
blocks.caption: Figure 2 Bad leaders can be found in both real life and fiction

blocks.text: Researchers have defined many types of negative leadership, often with different terminology. Two key categories follow: **ineffective** and **destructive** leadership.

Barbara Kellerman (2004) defines seven types of bad leadership in *Bad Leadership: What it is, How it Happens, Why it Matters*, using many high-profile case studies. She first divides bad leadership into two broad categories:

'Fails to produce the desired change. For reasons that include missing traits, weak skills, strategies badly conceived, and tactics badly employed, ineffective leadership falls short of its intention.'
blocks.title: Ineffective leadership

blocks.text: 'Fails to distinguish between right and wrong.'
blocks.title: Unethical leadership

blocks.text: This course concentrates on the first category, ineffective leadership.
Kellerman (2004) divides ineffective leadership into three groups, each illustrated with case studies:

head: Type
Description
Case study
rows: Lacks the will or skill (or both) to sustain effective action; does not create positive change
Stiff and unyielding; unable or unwilling to adapt to new ideas, new information or changing times
Lacks self-control and is aided and abetted by followers who are unwilling or unable to intervene

blocks.text: A growing body of research focuses on **destructive leadership**. After a comprehensive literature review, Padilla, Hogan and Kaiser (2007) set out five features:

items: It is seldom absolutely or entirely destructive: there are both good and bad results in most leadership situations.
It involves dominance, coercion and manipulation rather than influence, persuasion and commitment.
It has a selfish orientation, focused more on the leader's needs than those of the larger social group.
Its effects compromise the quality of life for constituents and detract from the organisation's main purposes.
Destructive outcomes are not only the result of destructive leaders, but also of susceptible followers and conducive environments.

blocks.text: A more recent literature review and meta-analysis of over 400 data samples (Mackey et al., 2021) suggests we still have an incomplete understanding of destructive leadership, and aims to provide a foundation for further research into the wide variety of destructive styles and behaviours now defined.

Their paper lists **21 definitions** of destructive leadership styles from the literature, ranging from **aversive leadership** (leading through intimidation, threats and punishment) to **leadership incivility** (leaders displaying a lack of regard for followers).
Have you ever encountered a leader who falls into one of these categories? Can you recognise any of those characteristics in yourself?
blocks.title: Reflect

blocks.alt: A Theranos company building with the company sign in front
blocks.caption: Figure 3 Biotech company, Theranos

blocks.text: Elizabeth Holmes was CEO of biotech company Theranos, which claimed a new technology could run hundreds of tests on small blood samples, speeding up diagnosis and treatment. The technology never worked successfully, and Holmes received a prison sentence for fraud. Tourish (2023) draws out examples of bad leadership:

items: The Board Holmes appointed was high profile across US society but had no biotech expertise, so no one offered expertise, oversight and feedback on key decisions.
The leadership style was controlling, using surveillance cameras and strict limits on colleagues sharing information.
Employees who asked too many questions or wouldn't 'show unmitigated loyalty' were encouraged to leave.

blocks.text: Holmes has been described as both a destructive leader and a **negatively charismatic** leader: one who used their natural charisma in a destructive way.

blocks.title: Match each description to the type of poor leadership

pairs.def: Lacks the will or skill (or both) to sustain effective action
Unable or unwilling to adapt to new ideas, information or changing times
Lacks self-control, aided by followers who will not or cannot intervene
Fails to distinguish between right and wrong
Leading through intimidation, threats and punishment
Leaders displaying a lack of regard for followers
Using natural charisma in a destructive way

blocks.title: Activity 2 Categorising poor leadership
blocks.prompt: Refer to the example of poor leadership you thought of in Activity 1. Looking at the types and definitions in this section, can you fit that leader into any of the categories? Summarise your thoughts.
blocks.model: Did your example fit Kellerman's ineffective leadership category - incompetent, rigid or intemperate? Or was your leader destructive, or even negatively charismatic? A key question is: what can I learn from that person's approach to make sure it isn't a path I take in my own leadership career? If your leader is neither ineffective nor destructive, they may simply be making common leadership mistakes.
points: Test the example against incompetent, rigid and intemperate.
Consider whether it was destructive or negatively charismatic.
Ask what you can learn so you don't follow the same path.
Some poor leaders are simply making common mistakes.

blocks.text: Both Kellerman (2004) and Padilla et al. (2007) include **followers** in their definitions of poor or bad leadership: bad or destructive leaders can't have the same impact without **bystanders** who look the other way, or **colluders** who join in the destruction.

Analysis by Mackey et al. (2021) shows 'that much of destructive leadership research actually examines subordinates' negative perceptions of their supervisors instead of how destructive leaders impact followers and their organisations.'
You'll investigate followership in more detail in Week 5. Next, you'll consider the impact of poor leadership on individuals, teams and businesses.

pages.title: Activity 3: The impact of poor leadership

blocks.alt: A pane of glass with cracks radiating out from an impact at its centre
blocks.caption: Figure 4 Poor leadership can be shattering

blocks.title: Activity 3 Impact of poor leadership
blocks.prompt: Think of a time when you felt demotivated. Could your leader (manager, supervisor, team captain etc.) have done anything to change how you felt? What could they have done? What could you have done yourself to change the situation?
blocks.model: Demotivation is a common result of poor leadership, but a leader can do something about it - acknowledging the demotivation and taking steps to boost morale is a good start. You could also act yourself: giving your leader appropriate, constructive feedback can lead to a positive outcome for everyone. In extreme circumstances, such as bullying or harassment, you may need support from Human Resources.
points: Demotivation is a common result of poor leadership.
A leader can acknowledge demotivation and boost morale.
Followers can give the leader constructive feedback.
In extreme cases like bullying or harassment, seek HR support.

blocks.text: In their meta-analysis of destructive leadership, Schyns and Schilling (2013) propose a framework of four concepts:

head: Area
Impact
rows: Followers resist the leader (e.g. ignoring requests) and lose trust in them
Job satisfaction diminishes as the environment becomes less pleasant; followers become less dedicated or motivated
Commitment falls as followers feel the organisation failed to protect them; productivity and turnover are affected
Followers experience stress and harm to well-being; they reduce effort, leading to poor performance

blocks.text: Cao et al. (2022) found that destructive leadership was most strongly associated with increased **workplace aggression**, while ethical leadership had the strongest negative association - suggesting that 'the emerging leadership types […] have considerable added value.'

Lucy was a Head of Department in a school, an effective leader with a dedicated team and a strong relationship with the Headteacher. Then the school came under pressure for better results, and the stressed Headteacher began making unrealistic demands. Lucy resisted and argued for a different approach; he became increasingly autocratic, telling her what to do and criticising work he had previously been happy with. She felt she had to follow his instructions. Her team could see she lacked conviction when passing on his demands, assumed she had lost interest and wasn't fighting their corner, and lost respect for her; many became demotivated and critical. Lucy lost confidence, communicated less with her team and became intimidated by her boss, which increased his frustration. Feeling unsupported by both, she eventually left the school.

blocks.title: Activity 4 Case study
blocks.prompt: Answer: 1) Was the Headteacher a destructive leader? 2) What could Lucy have done differently? 3) How might Lucy have maintained the motivation of her team? 4) Might members of the team have viewed Lucy as a destructive leader?
blocks.model: Many circumstances can lead to destructive leadership; here increasing pressure caused the Headteacher to behave destructively, and a lack of emotional intelligence meant he didn't see his impact on Lucy. Lucy could have been clearer with her team about her efforts to counter his demands, and discussed ways to convince him using the team's ideas. She might have sought support from other Heads of Department, HR, school governors or the local authority. Her team might have viewed her leadership as 'incompetent', based on poorly informed assumptions.
points: Pressure led the Headteacher to behave destructively, and he lacked emotional intelligence.
Lucy could have been open with her team about her efforts and involved them.
She could have sought support from peers, HR, governors or the local authority.
The team may have seen Lucy as incompetent because they lacked information.

blocks.alt: A man in a suit covering his face, surrounded by fingers pointing at him
blocks.caption: Figure 5 All leaders will make mistakes

blocks.text: You don't have to be a poor leader to make mistakes. All leaders have good and bad outcomes throughout their careers, however good their intentions. The point is to **learn from mistakes** - and, better still, from other people's before you make them yourself.

blocks.title: Rebecca Fielding: mistakes and the three-step model
blocks.note: Rebecca says every leader makes mistakes, especially early on, under pressure or on a steep learning curve - and that's OK. As soon as you recognise a mistake, share it with someone you trust and decide how to rectify it. It's fine to say: 'I made the best decision I could with the information I had; I now have new information and have made a different decision.' Her three-step model: 1) feel the pain - the embarrassment, frustration or worry; 2) take the lesson and attach it to that pain, so your brain learns (like a toddler touching a hot radiator); 3) the step everyone forgets - move on, let it go and move forward confidently, owning the mistake without being ashamed of it, and ask for help when you need it.

items: **Feel the pain** of the mistake.
**Learn the lesson** and attach it to that feeling.
**Move on** confidently - let it go.

blocks.text: Here are the first three of six common leadership mistakes. Propose possible solutions for each.

items: **Lack of clear vision:** your team doesn't know why they're doing something, what they're working towards or what success looks like. They lack direction and waste time.

**Poor communication:** individuals don't know what you want or whether they're doing a good job, so they feel uncertain and lack commitment. They don't know how to communicate with you, so they stop trying.
**Micromanagement and failure to delegate:** team members feel you don't trust or value them and are demotivated. They wait for instructions and show less initiative.

blocks.title: Activity 5 Common mistakes and possible solutions (part 1)
blocks.prompt: Propose possible solutions for: lack of clear vision; poor communication; micromanagement and failure to delegate.
blocks.model: Vision: be clear about what the team is working towards and what success looks like; communicate it regularly in different ways, keep the message concise, or involve the team in creating it. Communication: give timely praise or constructive feedback and be regularly available for discussion; understanding what motivates or concerns people builds mutual trust. Delegation: balance letting trusted team members take responsibility with overseeing progress, so people feel empowered and trusted.
points: Make the vision and what success looks like clear, and involve the team in shaping it.
Communicate regularly in different ways with a concise message.
Give timely praise and constructive feedback and be available to talk.
Delegate to trusted people while overseeing progress, so they feel empowered.
blocks.hint: Allow about 10 minutes for this part.

items: **Recruiting the wrong people:** people who lack key skills or have the wrong attitude can damage morale and progress. If you thought that person would fit in, what does that say about your opinion of everyone else?
**Failing to develop your team:** you haven't invested in upskilling them, yet your expectations keep growing. Employees feel unappreciated and out of their depth, losing confidence and motivation.

**Failing to lead by example:** you never attend their meetings or events, so they assume you aren't interested. You're always on your phone (business calls, but they don't know that). They start to copy your behaviour.

blocks.title: Activity 5 Common mistakes and possible solutions (part 2)
blocks.prompt: Propose possible solutions for: recruiting the wrong people; failing to develop your team; failing to lead by example.
blocks.model: Recruitment: take time to surround yourself with good people you can trust and delegate to, freeing you to maximise team performance. Development: learn the team's development needs and align them with your vision and plan; make sure everyone, including you, can develop - it could be work shadowing rather than an expensive course. Example: attend key team meetings and events, model the behaviours you want, work reasonable hours and check on anyone still in the office when you leave. Solutions depend on context; identifying and acknowledging the mistake is the starting point.
points: Recruit good people you can trust and delegate to.
Identify development needs and give everyone, including you, chances to develop.
Development need not be expensive, e.g. work shadowing.
Model the behaviours you expect, attend team events and keep a healthy work-life balance.
Acknowledging the mistake is the starting point for fixing it.
blocks.hint: Allow about 10 minutes for this part.

blocks.text: If you're worried about making mistakes, several avenues of support are available. Rebecca Fielding explains how employers support leaders and how leaders can support themselves.

blocks.title: Rebecca Fielding: support for leaders
blocks.note: Rebecca reiterates that mistakes are normal. Organisations support leaders through appraisal and performance reviews, and everyday feedback and coaching from line managers, peers and colleagues. You may be given a buddy (someone who has done the job), a coach (who helps you think through what happened and learn from it) or a mentor (someone more senior and experienced who shares their wisdom). There may be training courses and online resources such as badged open courses. She also recommends 'following your feet': TED talks, YouTube videos, books, and articles in your industry or sector press - follow what interests you, as it gives you energy and insight.

items: Appraisals and everyday feedback
A buddy, coach or mentor
Training courses and online resources
Your own reading and viewing

blocks.text: Much of the impact of poor leadership is felt by followers. From her case studies, Kellerman (2004) advises leaders who want to work more effectively with their teams to:

items: Establish a culture of openness in which diversity and dissent are encouraged.
Install an independent person to review complaints and maintain standards.
Bring in strong, independent advisers who aren't afraid to tell you the truth.
Avoid 'group think', as it discourages healthy dissent.
Get reliable and complete information, then disseminate it.
Give a senior manager who knows the organisation well responsibility for ensuring the mission continues to matter.
Establish checks and balances to avoid policies and procedures that support bad leadership.
Connect to all your constituents, not just a chosen, like-minded few.

blocks.text: For a follower on the receiving end of poor leadership, Kellerman advises:

items: Make bad leaders pay for their transgressions.
Find allies.
Develop your own sources of information - don't rely on what your leader provides.
Take collective action, e.g. get a small group together to talk to the boss.
Be a watchdog.
Hold leaders to account.

blocks.text: Don't let them get away with it. Whether you discuss the issue directly with your boss or escalate it appropriately, followers play a crucial role in leadership and business success - including when a leader is failing. Adapt these actions to your context.
blocks.title: Kellerman's key message

blocks.text: In Week 3 you looked at the skills a good leader needs. Now you'll focus on those a poor leader can lack, and how to develop them.

blocks.alt: 'Mind the gap' painted in yellow on the ground next to a railway track
blocks.caption: Figure 6 A gap in your leadership skills?

blocks.title: Activity 6 What skills were lacking?
blocks.prompt: Go back to the negative leadership example from Activity 1. Using the list of leadership skills from Week 3 (the personal skills audit) as a prompt, list the specific skills or abilities that leader didn't demonstrate.
blocks.model: Many instances of poor leadership relate to a lack of empathy or poor communication. Did you identify other areas for that person's development? Some skills may seem fixed, such as the ability to empathise, but experts agree that even the least empathetic person can learn to demonstrate empathy, even if it doesn't come naturally.
points: Poor leadership often involves a lack of empathy.
Poor communication is another common gap.
Look for other specific development areas for the leader.
Even skills that seem fixed, like empathy, can be learned.

blocks.text: The skills with most impact on leadership often involve how someone relates to, is perceived by and communicates with others. **Emotional intelligence** (Week 3) includes empathy, self-awareness and self-regulation - often missing or under-developed in the types of poor leadership covered this week. Bariso (2016) suggests seven steps to develop it:

items: Reflect on your own emotions
Ask others for perspective
Be observant
Use 'the pause': stop and think before you act
Explore the 'why', e.g. 'Why does that person feel the way they do?'; 'Why do I feel differently?'
When criticised, don't take offence; ask 'What can I learn?'
Practice, practice, practice.

blocks.text: Step 7 matters: these steps won't come naturally at first and need perseverance over time to become embedded.
**Integrity** is always high on the list in leadership skills surveys and recruitment. It can be seen as lacking in poor leaders, especially if they cover up mistakes or lack of ability with lies.

'Soundness of moral principle; the character of uncorrupted virtue, especially in relation to truth and fair dealing; uprightness, honesty.' (Oxford English Dictionary, 2023) - in short, always doing the right thing and being honest.
blocks.title: Integrity

blocks.text: Amster (2015) suggests: fulfil your promises; keep appointments; before you commit, reflect on whether you can deliver; get comfortable with saying no.

A Mind Tools (n.d.) editorial, 'Preserving integrity', suggests asking of every choice: *If my choice were printed on the front page of the newspaper, would I feel OK about it? If I make this choice, will I feel OK with myself afterwards?*

**Resilience** is an individual's ability to 'bounce back' from difficult and challenging situations. Without it, a leader can rapidly lose self-confidence and the ability to motivate others, soon becoming ineffective.
Lucy, Poorkavoos and Thompson (2014) set out five key factors of a resilient leader in their **Resilience Capabilities model**:

items: Perspective
Emotional intelligence
Purpose, values and strengths
Connections
Managing physical energy

blocks.text: The next pages give their reflective questions for each factor.
Perspective

items: Can you positively reframe negative experiences and find opportunity in adversity?
Can you accept what you cannot change, and focus on what you can?
Are you solution-driven, or do you get stuck in the problem?
Can you face negative information fully without dwelling on it?

blocks.text: Emotional intelligence

items: Do you acknowledge your own feelings and express them appropriately?
Can you change your mood when you need to?
How intentional are you about supporting others?

blocks.text: Purpose, values and strengths

items: Do you have a clear sense of purpose at work?
Do you know your personal strengths and use them regularly at work?
Do you know your values and act consistently with them?
Does your work fit your personal values and beliefs?

blocks.text: Connections

items: Do you have a strong, reliable network inside and outside work to help you through difficult times?
Can you meet your varied needs through a diverse support network?

blocks.text: Managing physical energy

items: Do you exercise regularly, get enough sleep and eat a healthy diet?
Do you make time for activities that give you joy or help you relax?

blocks.text: Managing physical energy, or taking care of yourself, is a key element of resilience that is often overlooked. How can you grow and lead your team through adversity if you're tired, unhealthy and stressed?
To explore resilience in the workplace in more detail, see the OpenLearn course 'Developing career resilience'.
blocks.title: Further study

blocks.text: This week you've considered the impact of poor leadership on followers. Next week, you'll look at the leader-follower relationship in more detail.
This is the Week 4 compulsory badge quiz: 15 questions instead of the usual 5. It counts towards your badge; if you're not successful first time, you can try again.

blocks.q: Kellerman (2004) first divides bad leadership into which two broad categories?
blocks.explain: Ineffective leadership fails to produce the desired change; unethical leadership fails to distinguish between right and wrong.

blocks.q: A leader who is stiff and unyielding, unable or unwilling to adapt to new ideas or changing times, is described by Kellerman as:
blocks.explain: Rigid leaders cannot or will not adapt to new ideas, information or changing times.

blocks.q: Which of Kellerman's types lacks self-control and is aided by followers unwilling or unable to intervene?
blocks.explain: Intemperate leadership lacks self-control and is enabled by followers who don't intervene.

blocks.q: According to Padilla, Hogan and Kaiser (2007), destructive leadership is usually entirely destructive, with no good results.
blocks.explain: Their first feature says destructive leadership is seldom absolutely or entirely destructive: most situations have both good and bad results.

blocks.q: According to Padilla et al. (2007), the process of destructive leadership involves:
blocks.explain: Destructive leadership relies on dominance, coercion and manipulation rather than influence, persuasion and commitment.

blocks.q: Padilla et al. (2007) say destructive organisational outcomes are the product of which factors? Select all that apply.
blocks.explain: Destructive outcomes are not only due to destructive leaders, but also susceptible followers and conducive environments.

blocks.q: In Mackey et al.'s (2021) review, 'aversive leadership' means:
options: Leaders displaying a lack of regard for followers
Leading through intimidation, threats and punishment
Using charisma in a destructive way
blocks.explain: Aversive leadership is leading through intimidation, threats and punishment; leadership incivility is a lack of regard for followers.

blocks.q: Which was NOT one of the examples of bad leadership at Theranos highlighted by Tourish (2023)?
options: A high-profile Board with no biotech expertise
A controlling style using surveillance cameras
Recruiting a strong independent adviser to challenge decisions
blocks.explain: The lack of independent expert oversight was part of the problem; the other three were cited as examples.

blocks.q: In Schyns and Schilling's (2013) framework, followers feeling the organisation failed to protect them, with effects on productivity and turnover, is:
blocks.explain: Organisation-related impacts include reduced commitment and effects on productivity and turnover.

blocks.q: Cao et al. (2022) found which type of leadership had the strongest negative association with workplace aggression?
blocks.explain: Destructive leadership was most strongly linked to increased aggression; ethical leadership had the strongest negative association.

blocks.q: What is the third step in Rebecca Fielding's model for dealing with a mistake - the one everyone forgets?
options: Attach the lesson to the pain
Move on, let it go and move forward confidently
blocks.explain: After feeling the pain and learning the lesson, you must let it go and move forward confidently.

blocks.q: A team doesn't know what they are working towards or what success looks like. Which common mistake is this?
blocks.explain: Lack of clear vision leaves the team without direction, wasting time on activities that may not be useful.

blocks.q: Which are among Kellerman's (2004) recommendations for leaders? Select all that apply.
options: Establish a culture where dissent is encouraged
Connect only with a like-minded few
Bring in independent advisers who will tell you the truth
blocks.explain: Kellerman advises connecting to all constituents, not just a chosen like-minded few.

blocks.q: In Bariso's (2016) steps for developing emotional intelligence, what is 'the pause'?
options: Stopping to think before you act
Waiting for others to speak first in meetings
Delaying decisions until all information is available
blocks.explain: 'The pause' means stopping and thinking before you act.

blocks.q: Which is one of the five factors in the Resilience Capabilities model (Lucy, Poorkavoos and Thompson, 2014)?
blocks.explain: The five factors are perspective; emotional intelligence; purpose, values and strengths; connections; and managing physical energy.

blocks.text: You should now have a better idea of what makes a poor leader and the negative impact of poor leadership, and you've considered how to rectify some of the common mistakes leaders make.
You should now feel that you can:

items: recognise poor leadership in different forms
reflect on the impact of poor or weak leadership
describe ways in which leadership mistakes might be avoided.

blocks.text: You are now halfway through the course. Next week you'll change perspective and look at leadership from the follower's point of view, then consider your own followers and how you might develop them.

chapters.title: Week 5: Why is followership important?
chapters.summary: Follower types, the benefits of good followership, what followers need, and how leaders can engage and develop them.

blocks.text: Last week you looked at what you can learn from bad leadership and the common mistakes leaders make. This week focuses on **followers** and the part they play in effective organisations.

items: Mainly interested in leadership? Many qualities of a proactive follower are the same as those of an effective leader.
Not much leadership experience yet? Becoming an effective follower is an excellent starting point.
Already a leader? You'll look at how to develop positive relationships with your followers and encourage them to consider their own leadership journey.

blocks.title: Lynne Johnson introduces Week 5
blocks.note: Lynne explains that this week you'll look at various types of followers, such as passive, alienated and conformist, and figure out what kinds of followers you currently have. You'll explore how to engage and develop your followers, and there is a short quiz at the end of the week.

blocks.title: By the end of this week you will be able to
blocks.text: recognise different types of followership; describe the benefits of effective followership; identify followers' needs; describe ways of engaging and developing your followers.
As you saw in Week 1, followership has been studied since the 1950s. Early work was mostly **leader-centred**, framing followers as recipients of leadership.

blocks.alt: Seven large birds fly in a V-shaped formation, a single bird leading and the others following.
blocks.caption: Figure 1 Followers have an important role to play

blocks.text: The body of research keeps growing and now takes a more **follower-centred** approach, investigating the interdependence between followers and leaders. Understanding the characteristics of different followers can make you a better follower *and* a better leader.
Several follower typologies exist, mainly leader-centred. One of the earliest and most widely cited is by Robert Kelley (1988), who describes five groups:

items: **Sheep** - passive and uncritical, lacking in initiative and a sense of responsibility. They perform the tasks given to them and stop.
**Yes people** - livelier but equally unenterprising. Dependent on a leader for inspiration, they can be aggressively deferential, even servile. Kelley later called them 'conformist followers'.

**Alienated followers** - critical and independent in their thinking but passive in carrying out their role. Often cynical, they sink gradually into disgruntled acquiescence, seldom openly opposing a leader.
**Survivors** - perpetually sample the wind and live by the slogan 'better safe than sorry'. They are adept at surviving change.
**Effective followers** - think for themselves and carry out their duties and assignments with energy and assertiveness.

blocks.text: Followership is not a person but a role ... effective followers and effective leaders are often the same people playing different parts at different hours of the day.
Match each description to the follower type Kelley (1988) gives it.

blocks.title: Match each description to Kelley's follower type

pairs.def: Passive and uncritical; they perform the tasks given to them and stop
Lively but unenterprising; dependent on the leader for inspiration and can be servile
Critical and independent thinkers, but passive and often cynical in their role
Perpetually sample the wind; 'better safe than sorry'
Think for themselves and carry out their duties with energy and assertiveness

blocks.text: Ira Chaleff (2009) bases his typology on two dimensions: how much a follower **supports** the leader and how much they **challenge** them. He describes four styles of followership:

head: Style
Support / challenge
What it looks like
rows: Does what's required but doesn't go beyond the minimum
Has low deference and isn't afraid to criticise
Does what is needed with minimal oversight or explanation
Gives vigorous support but is also willing to question the leader

blocks.q: In Chaleff's typology, which follower gives vigorous support but is also willing to question the leader?
blocks.explain: The partner combines high support with high challenge. The implementer is high support but low challenge.

pages.title: Carsten et al.: a follower-centred view

blocks.text: Much research looks at how follower styles support or derail *leadership*. Carsten et al. (2010) took a **follower-centred** approach, exploring how style and behaviour affect *followership itself*. They asked people about their role as follower - positives, negatives, personal qualities and behaviours - and grouped the answers into three categories:

items: **Passive** - taking and following orders, and deferring to the leader's knowledge and expertise.
**Active** - offering opinions when given the opportunity but remaining loyal and obedient whether or not they agreed with the leader.
**Proactive** - behaviours more aligned with partnership than dominance and submission.

blocks.text: 'Followership holds a multiplicity of meaning for individuals occupying the role' (Carsten et al., p. 21). Context matters: it depends on leadership style and the working environment.

pages.title: What type of follower are you?

blocks.text: So far you've considered what type of leader you are, or could be - but how many of us ever think about what type of follower we are? Identifying your own follower type makes you more aware of how you and others interact with leaders, which is useful when reflecting on your own role as a leader.

blocks.title: Activity 1 What type of follower are you?
blocks.prompt: In Week 1, Activity 2, you thought about your reasons for following various leaders. Choose one of those leader-follower relationships and, using the typologies in this section (Kelley; Chaleff; Carsten et al.), consider what type of follower you are. Summarise your thoughts.
blocks.hint: Name the typology and the type, give an example of your behaviour, and think about what shapes your engagement (the leader, the context).
blocks.model: Your follower type may stem from your personal qualities, but Bastardoz and Van Vugt (2019) suggest followers may match their style to their leader's, with engagement resulting from satisfaction with outcomes, fairness of the leader's procedures, alternative leaders and investment in the relationship. Context matters too: a sudden funding cut is likely to affect engagement. If you are not an effective follower, consider why and what would help; if you are, what inspires you and how you benefit. To improve, set a goal, e.g. give appropriate, constructive feedback to your leader within the next month, and note ideas in your leadership journal (the GROW goal-setting tool may help).
points: Identifies a specific follower type from one of the typologies
Supports it with an example of their own behaviour in a real leader-follower relationship
Considers how the leader's style or the context affects their engagement
Reflects on whether they are an effective follower and what would help them become more engaged
Sets a goal or next step for becoming a more effective follower

pages.title: How to develop as a follower

blocks.text: Across these typologies, positive or proactive followership means having energy and assertiveness, providing support but being willing to question, and seeing yourself as a **partner** rather than a subordinate.

But Benson et al. (2016), working with leaders of highly competitive sports teams, warn that leaders may interpret proactive behaviour differently in different situations. Five factors matter (p. 960):

items: the presence of third party observers
the momentary demands of the task at hand
the stage of the decision making process
suitability of the targeted issue
relational dynamics.

blocks.text: Proactive followership takes skill: recognise when your contributions are appropriate, or the leader may interpret them negatively.
Whether a follower is good or not is not just a matter of activity, but also depends on whether they assist the organisation in achieving its objectives or not.
A follower may be very proactive 'but in the opposite direction to what the organisation requires.'

blocks.title: Professor Jean Hartley: how to be a good follower
blocks.note: Being a good follower shares characteristics with being a good leader: think about yourself, the people you work with and the context. Think hard about your leader: what kind of person are they, what are they trying to achieve, what helps or hinders them, what are their preferences? Do they decide from figures and performance data or like stories; good news first or everything on the table; detail or the big picture? Start with what your leader most wants from a situation, then follow up with what you think is important. See yourself as one of several followers: take the initiative, volunteer, and present questions or problems constructively rather than obstructively. If you lead others, reflect on which of your own followers are helpful and constructive and apply that at the level above you.

pages.title: Try it: what kind of follower are you?

blocks.title: Try it: followership explorer
blocks.intro: Rate twelve statements about how you follow one particular leader to see where you sit on Kelley's, Chaleff's and Carsten et al.'s models, with development tips. Then explore the types and sort fifteen real follower behaviours.

blocks.text: Good followership benefits both followers and leaders. When they work effectively together, the organisation benefits too. Leaders and organisations clearly gain from effective, engaged employees - but followers gain as well, especially if they want to develop as future leaders.

blocks.alt: Four shiny silver cogs, each held in someone's hand, interlocking in the centre.
blocks.caption: Figure 2 When followers and leaders work well together there are many benefits

blocks.text: The typologies labelled good followers 'effective', 'proactive' or 'partners'. As leaders increasingly value these partnerships, followers should be aware of the benefits to them.

A follower with an effective relationship with their leader can influence situations where they think the leader is making a mistake, offer extra support, and improve circumstances for themselves and colleagues. This is sometimes called **'managing up'**.
Kipnis and Schmidt (1983) identify four strategies commonly used to influence superiors:

items: *Reason* - using data and information to support your requests
*Coalition* - mobilising others to support you
*Ingratiation* - creating goodwill
*Bargaining* - negotiating and exchanging benefits or favours.

blocks.q: Kipnis and Schmidt's four influencing strategies are used only by followers trying to influence their superiors.
blocks.explain: Leaders also use these strategies to influence their followers; they are just deployed in a different way.

blocks.title: Activity 2 Influencing up
blocks.prompt: Think of a time when you've tried to influence someone who was senior to you. What strategy did you use - reason, coalition, ingratiation or bargaining? Was it successful? If it wasn't, might one of the other strategies have worked better?
blocks.model: As Professor Hartley explains, the most successful approach depends on the person you are trying to influence: one person may respond better to a logical argument backed by data, another to the bigger picture. These four are not the only strategies; depending on the problem you may need to enlist the support of a more senior member of staff, or use recognised organisational policies and processes to highlight an issue.
points: Describes a real attempt to influence someone senior
Names the strategy used (reason, coalition, ingratiation or bargaining)
Evaluates whether it worked and why
Considers whether another strategy would have suited that person's preferences better

blocks.text: To explore this further, the course Toolkit includes a 'Managing your Manager' tool to help you understand your boss and their context.

pages.title: Benefit for followers: developing leadership skills

blocks.text: As a follower you can develop yourself as a future leader - by observing your leader's strengths and weaknesses, or through the support, advice and development opportunities they give you. Many skills of an effective follower are mirrored in an effective leader:

items: courage
judgement
communication
independent thinking
initiative
self-awareness and self-management
commitment
diplomacy
collaboration
influencing.

blocks.text: Agho (2009) surveyed over 300 senior executives: 'a significant number of the respondents agreed that followership skills should be viewed as prerequisites for effective leadership' (p. 7).

pages.title: Benefits for the organisation: more effective leadership

blocks.text: A more engaged and committed workforce benefits the organisation in many ways: leaders' and managers' work becomes easier and more rewarding, and business enhancements follow. A leader with a disengaged, unmotivated team finds it hard to complete projects, innovate or introduce change; engaged, enthusiastic followers make a huge difference.

blocks.title: Activity 3 What's in it for the leader?
blocks.prompt: Consider how a strong, engaged, enthusiastic team can benefit their leader, and list your ideas.
blocks.model: When your followers are engaged, your leadership is more effective. Followers who use their initiative and look for responsibility free up your time to focus more strategically. Engaged, enthusiastic team members are inspiring to work with, making your own role more enjoyable and fulfilling. And followers willing to challenge you could save you from some of the common leadership mistakes from Week 4.
points: Engaged followers make leadership more effective
Followers who take initiative free the leader's time for strategic work
An enthusiastic team makes the leader's role more enjoyable and fulfilling
Followers who challenge can save the leader from common mistakes

pages.title: Which followers does the organisation need?

blocks.text: A leader must think strategically about the types of followers their organisation needs - you might not always need 'effective' or 'proactive' followers. As Chaleff (2009) explains, an 'implementer' might seem the perfect follower, but if a leader starts making mistakes, the implementer is unlikely to challenge them. Some contexts, such as a manufacturing production line, benefit from passive followers who are happy to abide by the rules.

blocks.q: According to Chaleff (2009), what is the risk of a team made up of 'implementers'?
options: They are unlikely to challenge a leader who starts making mistakes
They will criticise every decision the leader makes
They will do only the bare minimum
blocks.explain: Implementers are high support/low challenge, so they do what is needed but rarely question the leader - even when the leader is going wrong.

blocks.text: **Employee engagement** is an increasingly popular management concept focusing on the mutual benefits of a strong relationship between employer and employee. The CIPD lists its benefits as:

items: Happier, healthier and more fulfilled employees
Better staff retention
Improved business performance, e.g. increased customer satisfaction, productivity, innovation, efficiency
Increased profit
Stronger brand and reputation.

blocks.text: So the benefits of good followership reach the follower, the leader and the organisation. Yet some organisations are starting to question whether the traditional leader-follower relationship is the most effective approach.

pages.title: Can you be a leader without followers?

blocks.text: Answers vary: some commentators give an emphatic 'no', while others ask whether there needs to be a leader at all.

blocks.alt: An empty lecture theatre with tiered blue seats and white walls.
blocks.caption: Figure 3 Can you lead if you have no followers?

blocks.text: Reviewing the literature, Uhl-Bien et al. (2014) find two key approaches in followership research:

items: *Followership as a position or role* - how followers' identities and behaviours influence leader attitudes, behaviours and outcomes.
*Followership as a social process* - followership and leadership are co-constructed in social and relational interactions between people.

blocks.text: In both, followership and leadership are closely linked, each influencing the other to create the best outcomes.

pages.title: Where have all the followers gone?

blocks.text: Kempster et al. (2020) interviewed Executive MBA students and found an 'absence of follower identification in their everyday working lives'. They ask:
Can we, as researchers, label practices as leading or following and label our research subjects as leaders or followers if they themselves reject those identifications?

They discuss more fluid forms such as distributed and collective leadership: 'a flow between people leading and following - rather than designated, materialised leaders permanently leading and followers following.'

blocks.q: Uhl-Bien et al. (2014) describe followership as a social process in which leadership and followership are co-constructed through relationships.
blocks.explain: This is the second of their two approaches; the first treats followership as a position or role.

blocks.title: Leadership from a dancing guy
blocks.note: A man is dancing on his own and others are gradually encouraged to join him until everyone wants to take part.

blocks.title: Activity 4 Leadership from a dancing guy
blocks.prompt: Watch the video and consider what characteristics the man exhibits that persuade others to participate. Make a list of your observations.
blocks.model: The man's enthusiasm and commitment to his activity is infectious. Once people start to join him, the mood changes and everyone wants to participate. Anyone can start something without followers, but with a clear vision that is easy to follow, followers will join. At work, a project that starts off unpopular can win people over if you communicate well and inspire them; convincing one or two team members first means they may advocate for you across the wider team.
points: Enthusiasm and commitment are infectious
Once the first followers join, the mood changes and others follow
A clear vision that is easy to follow attracts followers
Winning over one or two early supporters can bring the wider team on board

blocks.text: Followers play a key role in leadership success, but some approaches blur the traditional roles of leader and follower.

blocks.title: Shared leadership
blocks.text: 'A dynamic, interactive influence process among individuals in groups for which the objective is to lead one another to the achievement of group or organizational goals or both' (Pearce and Conger, 2003, p. 1).

Leadership behaviours are shown by a set of individuals rather than a single person; leadership becomes a shared function or activity rather than a role. It can create a strong sense of shared responsibility and effective collaboration, but relies on excellent communication - without it, decision-making can be impeded. It suits complex, technical environments where different experts in a multidisciplinary team become relevant at different stages of a project.
Other versions of shared leadership you may meet:

items: **Collective leadership** - 'a group of people with diverse skills and experience come together to work toward goals that they develop jointly... the group empowers the person or people with the most relevant expertise to tackle particular problems and implement solutions' (Shonk, 2023).
**Distributed leadership** - 'collaborative, autonomous practices managed by a network of formal and informal leaders across an organization' (Ancona, quoted in Somers, 2022).
**Holacracy** - a more radical approach that distributes leadership between all employees, removing the traditional leader-follower relationship altogether (more in Week 7).

blocks.title: Match each description to its approach

pairs.def: A dynamic, interactive influence process in which group members lead one another to achieve goals
A diverse group sets goals jointly and empowers those with the most relevant expertise to tackle problems
Collaborative, autonomous practices managed by a network of formal and informal leaders
Leadership distributed between all employees, removing the leader-follower relationship altogether

blocks.text: Even within these approaches, each individual has needs and responsibilities that require nurturing. Understanding and meeting your followers' needs lets you form positive relationships with your team.

blocks.alt: A hand holding a pen that has written 'What do you need?' on the front of a ring-bound notebook.
blocks.caption: Figure 4 Followers' needs are important

blocks.text: Jackson and Parry (2011) describe needs the leader must try to fulfil, for example:

items: the need for **clarity** - what should we be doing? Where are we going?
the need for **meaning** - what are we doing this for?
the need for **safety** - will it be ok if we do this?

blocks.text: A Gallup team asked over 10 000 followers what the most influential leaders contribute to their lives. Rath and Conchie (2008) identified four basic needs: **trust, compassion, stability and hope**. The researchers explained (Robison, 2009):

items: Trust: 'primarily built through relationships... the foundational currency that a leader has with his team or his followers.'
Stability: leaders should think constantly about creating 'a basic sense of security and stability throughout an organization.'
Hope: 'Followers need to see how things will get better... Leaders need to build that foundation of stability, and hope sits on top of that.'
Compassion: 'You can show you care, for example, by having tough conversations with people about their performance and their positioning.'

blocks.q: Which set lists the four basic needs of followers identified by Gallup's research (Rath and Conchie, 2008)?
blocks.explain: Gallup's research with over 10 000 followers found trust, compassion, stability and hope. Clarity, meaning and safety come from Jackson and Parry (2011).

pages.title: Identifying the needs of your followers

blocks.text: Considering the needs of different types of follower lets you interact with current followers more effectively, or prepares you for future leadership and helps you pre-empt issues.

blocks.title: Activity 5 Identifying the needs of your followers
blocks.prompt: Choose a typology and think of examples of different types of followers you have encountered (if you don't lead anyone, think about a leader you follow and your fellow followers). Then answer: (1) Did you observe behaviours that were positive or negative? (2) What were the reasons for their engagement or lack of it? (3) What do you think those followers needed? (4) What actions did the leader take to identify those needs - and what could they have taken?
blocks.model: The followers may share a common type or you may have identified a range of types. Their needs might be the same but expressed differently, or there may be a range of issues to address. Look for common themes that could be addressed with the whole team, and use your leadership journal to explore issues in more detail.
points: Uses a named typology to describe real followers
Identifies positive or negative behaviours and reasons for (dis)engagement
Names specific needs, e.g. clarity, meaning, safety, trust, compassion, stability or hope
Evaluates what the leader did, or could have done, to identify those needs
Looks for common themes that could be addressed with the whole team

blocks.text: In a large team you may not be able to address everyone's needs individually, but you can facilitate or delegate group activities and communication strategies.

A positive step towards engaging followers is to emphasise your commitment to their development. A team that is motivated and feels valued performs more effectively than one whose members feel underappreciated and ignored.

blocks.title: Professor Jean Hartley: engaging your followers
blocks.note: Followers have talents and initiative beyond their formal role description. Some people do exactly what they're asked and not a jot more - and are entitled to - but you'll get much more if people feel appreciated, respected and that you want their views and ideas on doing the task better. Drawing on the team brings in more perspectives and ideas you hadn't thought of. A high-energy team inspires energy in the leader and others; a 'dead' team with suppressed energy and poor communication is much harder to lead. The leader's task is to channel and focus that energy on the task, and care for people, rather than trying to control it.

blocks.text: Gallup's State of the Global Workplace report (2023) found:

head: Category (2022)
Share
Description
rows: Highest level since measurements began in 2009
'Filling a seat and watching the clock', feeling lost and disconnected
Taking actions that directly harm the organisation, 'undercutting its goals and opposing its leaders'; trust has been broken

blocks.text: Gallup estimates that 'low engagement costs the global economy US$8.8 trillion and accounts for 9% of global GDP' - so engagement matters for economic as well as individual productivity and success.

blocks.q: According to Gallup (2023), roughly what share of the world's employees were 'quiet quitting' in 2022?
blocks.explain: 59% were quiet quitting, 23% were thriving and engaged and 18% were loud quitting. 9% is the share of global GDP that low engagement is estimated to cost.

blocks.text: MacLeod and Clarke (2009) set out four enablers of employee engagement:

items: **Leadership** - a strong strategic narrative with widespread ownership: a clear story of the organisation's purpose, why it has its vision, and how each individual contributes. Employees have a clear line of sight between their job and the narrative.
**Engaging managers** - facilitate and empower rather than control; treat staff with appreciation and respect; commit to developing, increasing and rewarding their capabilities.
**Employee voice** - views are sought, listened to and make a difference; employees speak out and challenge when appropriate; listening and responsiveness run through the organisation.
**Integrity** - behaviour throughout the organisation is consistent with stated values, leading to trust.

blocks.text: These themes run through the course: Week 4's solutions (clear vision, good communication, developing your team, leading by example) and Week 6's challenges of motivating and developing a team.

blocks.title: Match each description to MacLeod and Clarke's enabler

pairs.def: A strong strategic narrative so employees see where their job fits the organisation's purpose
Managers who facilitate and empower, and treat staff with appreciation and respect
Employees' views are sought and listened to, and they challenge when appropriate
Behaviour throughout the organisation is consistent with stated values

blocks.title: Professor Jean Hartley: task and context
blocks.note: Make sure people are clear about the task and their contribution to it: check they understand it and ask whether they have better ideas for carrying it out - a sense of purpose is very important. Also help manage the wider context the team operates in: share enough for people to see where their work fits, but protect them from context that is distracting or distressing. She tells a (possibly apocryphal) NASA story: a visiting dignitary asked a cleaner about their job and was told 'my job is to help put men on the Moon' - knowing where your job fits the bigger purpose can be incredibly motivating.

blocks.text: Link this to MacLeod and Clarke's first enabler: employees need a clear line of sight between their job and the organisation's narrative.
Kelley (1988) notes that many organisations train leaders but few train followers. He outlines topics for a follower training programme:

items: Improving independent, critical thinking
Self-management
Disagreeing agreeably
Building credibility
Aligning personal and organisational goals and commitments
Acting responsibly towards the organisation, the leader, co-workers and oneself
Similarities and differences between leadership and followership roles
Moving between the two roles with ease.

blocks.text: More recently, Oc et al. (2023) recommend that leadership development first focuses on 'how a group of individuals interact with each other' and their shared objective, before 'the things they need to do to achieve that objective'. Leaders and followers must 'learn how leadership can be shared and how the roles they play can change depending on the circumstances' (p. 18).

pages.title: Other ways to support your followers

blocks.text: As well as training and development opportunities, you can:

items: Allow them to take responsibility and lead on different elements of the work.
Give praise and encouragement, acknowledging their work and taking a step back yourself.
Give them confidence to innovate by letting them implement changes without fear of repercussions.
Coach them using your knowledge and experience - or coach key individuals who can cascade your knowledge to others.

blocks.title: The follower's view
blocks.text: Followers may resist development if they feel you ask too much - e.g. they aren't paid enough for more responsibility, or resent delegated tasks they aren't interested in. Plan development *with* them: give them a voice and explain the business needs that must be addressed.

blocks.title: Activity 6 Developing your followers
blocks.prompt: Think about an individual or group you want to develop into more effective followers or prepare for future leadership - e.g. members of an existing team, a social group you want to inspire, or social media followers you want to build on Twitter or LinkedIn. How could you inspire or develop them? What could you do to explore their needs and expectations?
blocks.model: Identify the person or group clearly, then think about what they need and expect - ask them, rather than assume. Plan ways to inspire and develop them, such as giving responsibility, praise, freedom to innovate and coaching. Use your leadership journal to explore the ideas and form a plan, try to implement some aspect of follower development over the next few weeks and months, and use the GROW tool to plan your next steps.
points: Identifies a specific person or group to develop
Describes how to find out their needs and expectations, e.g. by talking with them
Proposes concrete ways to inspire or develop them
Plans next steps, such as a journal entry, GROW plan or timescale

blocks.text: Our understanding of followership and its interdependence with leadership is still developing, but even leader-centric studies show that followers play a vital role in leadership and business success. Followers should be nurtured and encouraged to interact - sometimes critically - with leaders, and leaders should reciprocate with feedback and dialogue. This boosts engagement and motivation and prepares followers for their own leadership roles.

blocks.title: You should now be able to
blocks.text: recognise different types of followership; describe the benefits of effective followership; identify followers' needs; describe ways of engaging and developing your followers.
Next week: common challenges for modern leaders - internal politics, team dynamics, leading change, and motivating and developing staff.

blocks.q: Which statement best reflects Kelley's (1988) view of followership?
options: Followership is a personality trait you are born with
Followership is a role; effective followers and leaders are often the same people at different times
Followers are simply recipients of leadership
Good followers never question their leader
blocks.explain: Kelley argues 'followership is not a person but a role' - the same people play leader and follower parts at different hours of the day.

blocks.q: Which of these are among Kipnis and Schmidt's (1983) strategies for influencing superiors? Select all that apply.
blocks.explain: The four strategies are reason, coalition, ingratiation and bargaining. Intimidation is not one of them.

blocks.q: Shared leadership works well even without excellent communication, because responsibility is spread across the group.
blocks.explain: Shared leadership relies on excellent communication; without it, it can impede decision-making.

blocks.q: Carsten et al. (2010) described followers who offer opinions when given the chance but stay loyal and obedient whether or not they agree. Which category is this?
blocks.explain: Active followers offer opinions but remain loyal and obedient regardless; proactive followers behave more like partners.

chapters.title: Week 6: Challenges for every leader
chapters.summary: Common leadership challenges - building teams, motivating and developing staff, leading change and dealing with internal politics - and ways to address them.

blocks.text: Last week you looked at followership from the perspectives of both follower and leader, and at the importance of follower engagement and development. This week focuses on key challenges leaders face - **building an effective team, dealing with internal politics, motivating and developing staff, and leading change** - and potential solutions to each.

blocks.title: Lynne Johnson introduces Week 6
blocks.note: Lynne explains that this week tackles fundamental leadership skills: how to build an effective team, deal with internal politics, motivate and develop your staff, and lead change. We often look to great leaders from history for inspiration - but does leadership change over time, and what are the challenges for modern leaders?

blocks.title: By the end of this week you will be able to
blocks.text: recognise a range of common leadership challenges; reflect on challenges you have observed or experienced; describe ways in which common leadership challenges might be addressed.

The role of leader is not an easy one. Leaders juggle and prioritise many complex responsibilities, and as leadership styles and employee expectations change they must increasingly prioritise staff **wellbeing**. Many leaders thrive on the variety, but it can be challenging.

blocks.alt: A snow-covered mountain peak.
blocks.caption: Figure 1 There are many challenges for modern leaders

blocks.text: Many researchers have surveyed leaders worldwide to identify common challenges. Before looking at the results, start with your own perceptions.

blocks.title: Activity 1 Three most critical leadership challenges
blocks.prompt: What are the three most critical leadership challenges you or your leaders currently face? List them.
blocks.model: Did you choose mainly internal or external challenges, or a mix? You may have focused on internal challenges such as building and motivating your team, or on national or global issues that could affect your leadership. The challenges different leaders face vary with the context of their work and their own strengths and abilities.
points: Lists three specific challenges
Distinguishes internal (e.g. team, motivation) from external (national or global) challenges
Recognises that challenges depend on context and the leader's own strengths and abilities

blocks.text: Online searches for the most common recent leadership challenges frequently mention:

items: leading a team
inspiring and motivating others
developing employees
dealing with change
fostering trust.

pages.title: Professor Hartley's view of the challenges

blocks.text: Jean Hartley has worked with many high-profile leaders, from elected politicians to civic activists and public and private sector professionals.

blocks.title: Professor Jean Hartley: common leadership challenges
blocks.note: Three challenges. (1) Be clear about the purpose or task of your leadership: even experienced leaders need to reflect carefully, continuously and critically on whether they have framed it right, broken down the tasks appropriately or missed something. (2) Match your leadership style or approach to the context, the people and the outcomes - e.g. senior police deciding between command and control in a public order emergency and drawing the whole team into problem solving for a new problem; is this new and unclear, needing all the brains and expertise available, or something done before, where the job is to deliver on time, to high quality, with people fulfilled? (3) Maintain 'grace under pressure': even when stressed or under attack from colleagues, a boss or the media, stay calm, good humoured, respectful and polite. A leader who loses their temper or snaps has 'lost it' to some extent.

blocks.text: In *Grace Under Pressure: Leading through Change and Crisis*, John Baldoni (2023) describes grace under pressure as meeting:

items: anger with composure
denigration with respect
sadness with compassion
scarcity with abundance
insults with smiles
selfishness with selflessness
hoarding with generosity
life with gratitude.

blocks.text: (Baldoni, 2023, p. xvii) - something for everyone to aspire to!

blocks.q: According to Baldoni (2023), grace under pressure means meeting anger with...
blocks.explain: Baldoni's list begins 'anger with composure', followed by denigration with respect, sadness with compassion and so on.

blocks.title: Activity 2 Personal leadership challenges
blocks.prompt: Reflect on your experiences of leadership challenge, as the leader or as an observer. Choose one example from the common challenges so far and summarise the situation. Then answer: What actions did the leader take? What actions did others take? What was the outcome?
blocks.model: Reflecting on your own times of challenge or crisis and your actions gives insight into your methods and whether you need to change them - use your leadership journal to do this regularly. If you observed another leader, you can learn from their strengths and weaknesses and apply what you learn to your own practice now or in the future.
points: Summarises a specific challenge linked to one of the common challenges
Describes the leader's actions and those of others
States the outcome
Draws a lesson about their own methods or what to apply in future

blocks.text: Leading a team is a significant part of any leader's role, and getting an increasingly diverse range of members to work well together can be a challenge. Bruce Tuckman's (1965) team development model, still widely referenced, has four stages:

items: **Forming** - members test boundaries and explore behaviours, getting to know each other. Your role: introduce members and roles, and describe the team's focus with clarity.
**Storming** - members push against boundaries, leading to conflict and emotional responses. Your role: mediate, using your authority when required, helping them recognise each other's work styles.
**Norming** - the group overcomes resistance and finds new cohesion. Your role: monitor progress and give constructive feedback and praise.
**Performing** - roles become flexible and functional; energy goes into the task. Your role: step back, delegate more and focus on developing the team.

blocks.alt: Several hands come together in a group high five.
blocks.caption: Figure 2 Building a strong team is essential

blocks.text: Tuckman later added **adjourning**: the team is reorganised for other projects or disbanded. This can be a time of uncertainty, perhaps even a sense of loss if the team performed well.

blocks.alt: Graph of team effectiveness over time: effectiveness dips from forming to a low at storming, rises through norming to a peak at performing, then falls slightly at adjourning.
blocks.caption: Figure 3 Tuckman's team development model

blocks.text: Recognising that storming is normal - and that with the right mediation it will end - can help you deal with personal feelings of frustration or negativity.

blocks.title: Match each description to Tuckman's stage

pairs.def: Members get to know each other; the leader introduces roles and describes the team's focus clearly
Members push against boundaries and conflict arises; the leader mediates
The group finds new cohesion; the leader monitors progress and gives feedback and praise
Roles are flexible and functional; the leader steps back, delegates and develops the team
The team is reorganised or disbanded, which can bring uncertainty or a sense of loss

pages.title: Tuckman in hybrid and virtual teams

blocks.text: Since COVID-19 many teams work in a hybrid way (more on hybrid working in Week 7). Hoffman (2022) observes, based on Tuckman's model:

items: **Forming** takes longer for virtual teams - find creative ways to connect, e.g. messaging apps or team celebrations, especially for new hires who may feel left out.
**Storming** - a virtual environment makes some feel more able to lash out and others more likely to withdraw; leaders need the right balance.
**Norming** - remote working boosts task productivity at the expense of spontaneous collaboration, so look for chances to encourage spontaneity.
**Performing** takes constant work virtually - people may take things out of context or struggle with communication; watch for signs.
**Adjourning** - people easily 'disappear' after a project; publicly acknowledge contributions and invite continued contact to combat home workers' loneliness.

blocks.text: There is lots of online advice about team dynamics, but the fundamentals can be distilled into:

items: **choosing the right people** - a good mix of skills and knowledge that complement each other and get the job done
making sure members are **clear about the task** and motivated to achieve it
**regular communication** - monitoring progress, giving feedback and celebrating success.

blocks.q: According to Hoffman (2022), remote working tends to increase spontaneous collaboration during the norming stage.
blocks.explain: Remote working leads to greater task productivity at the expense of spontaneous collaboration, so leaders must look for ways to encourage it.

blocks.text: Team building exercises range from moving blindfolded through an obstacle course guided by a team member who can see, to a sports competition - and hybrid working adds even more options. They let the team interact outside work and learn about each other, and let you observe strengths and weaknesses in a different setting.
Choose an exercise whose learning points clearly transfer back to the workplace. An activity seen as 'pointless' can demotivate the team and lose respect for the leader.
Brown (2016) gives three ways to set up exercises that create impact:

items: Identify what impact you need - e.g. spending time together, learning skills, accomplishing something.
Decide what type of 'different' you need - e.g. location, mix of people, activity.
Create something tangible - e.g. an action plan, a decision made.

blocks.title: Activity 3 A team building exercise
blocks.prompt: 1. Think of a team you are in (virtual or in person): (a) Is the purpose of the team clear? (b) Does it have the right mix of people/skills? (c) Are people in the right roles, using their strengths? (d) Are members motivated? (e) Which phase is it in - forming, storming, norming or performing? (f) What development could it benefit from? 2. With (f) in mind, devise a team building exercise that addresses that need, with a realistic budget, a purpose and a benefit back in the normal team situation.
blocks.hint: For ideas, the Venture Team Building website lists over 60 activities, and a Hoppier blog (Aite, 2023) suggests 20 virtual activities for fun and engagement.
blocks.model: A good answer diagnoses the team (purpose, mix, roles, motivation, Tuckman stage) and designs an exercise that targets the development need, with a clear impact, a useful 'different' element and a tangible output, within a realistic budget. Consider actually running it - volunteer at an away day or training afternoon. Afterwards, reflect in your leadership journal, collect feedback from participants and consider what to do differently; Gibbs' (1988) reflective cycle from Week 3 can structure that reflection.
points: Assesses the team's purpose, mix of skills, roles and motivation
Identifies the team's Tuckman stage
Names a specific development need
Designs an exercise with a clear purpose, realistic budget and transferable benefit
Plans to gather feedback and reflect afterwards

blocks.alt: Gibbs' reflective cycle: a series of boxes arranged in a circle and connected by clockwise arrows.
blocks.caption: Figure 4 Gibbs' reflective cycle - use it to reflect on how your exercise went

blocks.text: A motivated team knows what it is working towards and shares your enthusiasm and commitment. If they believe in and respect you, they will often follow you when not yet certain about something. Three elements help:

items: a clear vision that you believe in, and a focus on the impact of the work
regular and inspiring communication to the whole team, not just your direct reports
leading by example and making yourself visible and accessible to your team.

blocks.alt: A word cloud built around 'motivation', with words such as business, teamwork, success, attitude and positive.
blocks.caption: Figure 5 Key words that capture the essence of motivation

blocks.text: These matter just as much with virtual teams - especially being visible and accessible, which may need more creativity online.
Professor Jean Hartley agrees that communicating progress is crucial, and sometimes challenging, for keeping a team inspired and focused.

blocks.title: Professor Jean Hartley: communicating progress
blocks.note: Some leaders are good at developing a strategy or holding the initial meeting or workshops, but fall down on continuing to communicate the purpose and progress. Leaders often get bored hearing themselves repeat the same things because they have already taken it in - but repeating it (not ad nauseam) helps. People may hear the words without understanding them at first, may have been preoccupied early on, or may start to flag halfway through a project, when reminding them why the work matters is really important.

blocks.q: Professor Hartley suggests that once a leader has explained the purpose clearly at the start of a project, repeating it later is unnecessary.
blocks.explain: She argues repeating the purpose and progress on several occasions helps, because people may not have understood or listened at first, or may flag halfway through.

blocks.text: Before you can motivate your team, a useful starting point is to think about what motivates you.

blocks.title: Activity 4 What motivates you?
