blocks.prompt: Think about a professional situation in which you felt really motivated. What made you feel like that? How was your motivation demonstrated in your actions? Summarise the situation.
blocks.model: Different people feel and show motivation in different ways, so consider your team members' personality types when looking for signs that they are with you. Enthusiasm and commitment can show in many ways, from volunteering for extra tasks or responsibilities to quietly completing tasks on time or even early.
points: Describes a specific professional situation
Identifies what caused the motivation
Explains how the motivation showed in their actions
Recognises that others may show motivation differently

blocks.text: A key way to motivate people is to show interest in their circumstances: support and coach them, look at their career plan together and consider how to develop them. Development needn't mean a formal course - it could involve:

items: work shadowing or secondment to another department or organisation
a new, stretching responsibility, e.g. chairing a discussion group or delivering online training
letting a team member implement a new idea they have had
delegating some of your work - showing you trust them to represent you
encouraging someone to find or become a mentor, e.g. through virtual introductions between hybrid workers.

blocks.text: Use your leadership journal (Week 3, Activity 6) to reflect on which ideas suit your team. A motivated team is usually happier and more productive, leading to better staff retention and improved business performance (see Week 5).

blocks.alt: Quotation: 'Change is a threat when done to me, but an opportunity when done by me.' Rosabeth Moss Kanter, business strategist.
blocks.caption: Figure 6 A quote about change from a well-known business strategist

blocks.text: Change is one of the biggest issues for any modern leader. People are often reluctant to change, but organisations need almost constant transformation as the external environment develops fast. Motivation is key, so leaders must balance the organisation's needs with motivating the team to keep looking forward.

blocks.title: Video on leading change
blocks.note: An external YouTube video recommended at the start of the course's section on leading change, before Kotter's eight-step change process (the source does not describe its content).

blocks.text: John Kotter developed his eight-step process over several decades (*Leading Change*, 2012; *Accelerate*, 2014).

blocks.alt: Eight numbered circles around a central 'The big opportunity': create a sense of urgency, build a guiding coalition, form a strategic vision and initiatives, enlist a volunteer army, enable action by removing barriers, generate short-term wins, sustain acceleration, institute change.
blocks.caption: Figure 7 Kotter's eight step change process

items: *Create a sense of urgency* - inspire people to act, with passion and purpose, on a bold, aspirational opportunity.
*Build a guiding coalition* of effective people to guide, coordinate and communicate it.
*Form a strategic vision and initiatives* - clarify how the future will differ from the past and how initiatives linked to the vision will make it real.
*Enlist a volunteer army* - large-scale change needs many people who *want* to contribute and are unified in pursuing the goal.
*Enable action by removing barriers* that slow things down or block progress - clear the way to innovate, work nimbly across silos and generate impact quickly.
*Generate short-term wins* - recognise, collect and communicate them to track progress and energise volunteers to persist.
*Sustain acceleration* - after the first successes, use your growing credibility to keep improving systems, structures and policies until the vision is achieved.
*Institute change* - regularly articulate the connections between the new behaviours and organisational success until they replace old habits.

blocks.title: Match each description to Kotter's step

pairs.def: Inspire people to act with passion and purpose on a bold opportunity
Gather effective people to guide, coordinate and communicate the change
Rally many people who actively want to contribute to a common opportunity
Clear roadblocks so people can innovate and work across silos
Recognise and communicate early successes to energise people
Link new behaviours to organisational success until they replace old habits

blocks.title: Activity 5 Plan a change
blocks.prompt: Choose something you'd like to change (at work, in a voluntary organisation, or a process that needs updating) - or use this example: you run a small customer advice team in a local government office; appointments are 'drop-in only' within office hours and queues become huge, so you want to change the booking process. Make notes for each of Kotter's steps: 1 Why is it urgent and how will you create urgency? 2 Who is in your guiding coalition (different levels and spheres of influence)? 3 What is your vision, how will it improve things, and what initiatives support it? 4 Who must you influence and how will you persuade them? 5 What or who are the barriers? 6 What short-term wins can you share with supporters? 7 How will you keep the change moving, and what will you monitor? 8 How will you communicate success, to whom, and ensure it is maintained?
blocks.hint: Work through all eight steps in order; one or two sentences each is enough.
blocks.model: For the example: (1) Urgent because customer complaints about queues are rising and advisers can't meet everyone's needs, so they feel demotivated and under pressure. (2) Senior management, customers, influential advisers and the reception staff who deal with queues. (3) Vision: meet customer needs within one week of a request, and within 24 hours for urgent enquiries - reducing queues, setting realistic expectations and letting advisers plan, in line with office goals on customer service and staff stress; collect customer feedback on the proposals. (4) Get customers, advisers and reception on side through decision-making meetings, e.g. on which booking system to use. (5) An adviser strongly against it: listen in a one-to-one, or meet every adviser so she isn't singled out. (6) Win IT's support to build an online booking system and involve advisers in the requirements. (7) Set a clear timeline and give regular updates. (8) Share evidence of shorter waits and positive client feedback with all stakeholders, and check the system until fully adopted. Record your plan in your journal and talk it through with a colleague; the Plan Do Study Act tool offers an alternative structure for small-scale changes.
points: Explains why the change is urgent
Names a varied guiding coalition and the people to win over
States a clear vision with supporting initiatives
Identifies barriers or resistors and how to address them
Plans short-term wins, sustained momentum and how success will be communicated and maintained

blocks.text: Change is challenging partly because of the natural discomfort or even active resistance team members often show.

blocks.title: Force field analysis
blocks.text: A change management tool developed by Kurt Lewin (1951) that looks at the **drivers** and **resistors** of change.

blocks.title: MindTools: force field analysis
blocks.note: A short MindTools video explaining how force field analysis works, weighing the forces driving a change against the forces resisting it. It ends by pointing to an accompanying article on the MindTools website.

blocks.q: What does Lewin's force field analysis examine?
options: The stages a team goes through as it develops
The drivers and resistors of a change
The four strategies for influencing superiors
The eight steps of a change programme
blocks.explain: Force field analysis looks at the forces driving change and those resisting it. The other options describe Tuckman, Kipnis and Schmidt, and Kotter.

blocks.text: Trust is a key element of successful change: if your team trusts you, they are more likely to follow your lead. Change management consultant Wendy Hirsch explains why.

blocks.title: Wendy Hirsch: why trust matters in change
blocks.note: Organisational change can threaten trust, because we build trust from our experiences and change makes us re-evaluate. Trust is linked to positive risk-taking, going above and beyond and task performance. Leaders can build and maintain trust in three ways: demonstrate competence (the technical know-how, yours or your team's); show you care about how the change affects people, by talking with them in small groups and addressing concerns; and walk the talk, upholding your values even when things shift. Also: give people some input into decisions, communicate clearly and honestly throughout the change (not just at the start), and model humility and curiosity, making it OK to make mistakes as long as everyone learns and adapts.

blocks.q: Which of these is one of Wendy Hirsch's three ways for leaders to build trust during change?
options: Keep plans confidential until they are final
Communicate mainly at the launch of the change
blocks.explain: Her three ways are demonstrate competence, show that you care, and walk the talk. She also recommends communicating honestly throughout and making it OK to make mistakes.

blocks.text: Surveying over 750 leadership programme participants worldwide, Gentry (2016) identified **internal politics** - also called office or workplace politics - as a key challenge: the actions and behaviours of those competing for status or power at work.

blocks.alt: A pair of blue and black boxing gloves hanging against a dark brick wall.
blocks.caption: Figure 8 Internal politics

blocks.text: Office politics exist because:

items: individuals and teams compete for limited resources and use tactics to influence those in charge of finances
some people seek promotion and want to look better than colleagues
people are committed to their project or department and promote it, especially to senior managers
people with strong moral or ethical views share them and can be dismissive of those who disagree
personality types differ - confident, vocal people can frustrate those who prefer a quieter, measured approach.

blocks.text: Politics can take a lot of time and energy, but as a team leader you must engage, or your team may miss out on resources or profile. To do it with minimum time and energy:

items: Be part of several networks so you aren't seen as taking sides; prioritise senior managers' requests for help and be reliable.
Don't gossip, and don't rely on promises of confidentiality unless you know you can trust someone.
Don't be afraid to give timely, appropriate and constructive feedback to senior staff.
Communicate clearly and authentically; follow up important conversations with an email.
Know what you are trying to achieve and be ready to explain why it is best for the organisation.
Listen - understanding your organisation lets you align your priorities with other departments; collaboration is viewed positively by senior managers.

blocks.title: Professor Jean Hartley: mobilising people
blocks.note: Some definitions of leadership describe it as mobilising people's time, attention and resources to achieve outcomes. Think about who you need to get on board: your team, but also people across the organisation whose work overlaps with yours or who pass work to you. You may need to maintain your area's reputation and help others understand what your team contributes to the wider purpose. Map out your stakeholders - possibly including the public, customers and suppliers - and how to encourage them to understand and support your work.

blocks.q: When leading a team, it is best to stay out of the organisation's political discourse altogether.
blocks.explain: Leaders need to involve themselves, otherwise their team may miss out on much-needed resources or profile - but they can do it efficiently, e.g. by networking widely, communicating clearly and listening.

blocks.text: **Activity 6 What would you do?** Reputation plays a key part in office politics: if you are well regarded, people are more inclined to support you, collaborate and share funding. Even small decisions affect how you are perceived. Decide what you would prioritise.

blocks.q: An urgent email arrives from your manager needing immediate attention. At the same moment a colleague says your manager's boss phoned and wants you to call back as soon as possible. What do you do?
options: Phone the more senior manager back straight away - your boss can wait
Read your manager's email before you call their boss - it might contain relevant information
Deal with your manager's email first - they said it was urgent and you've no idea what the senior manager wants
blocks.explain: Prioritise your response to the senior manager, but if you have time to quickly view your boss's email, it could give you information that will enhance your phone call.

blocks.q: In a meeting you have an important point to make, but it contradicts a senior manager who is present - and their boss is attending too. What do you do?
options: Keep quiet but discuss it with the senior manager after the meeting
Make your point in a constructive and polite manner
Keep quiet and never make your point - you don't want to make enemies
blocks.explain: The textbook answer is to make your point constructively and politely: a good leader should respond positively to constructive disagreement, the senior leader may even agree, and others will gain a favourable impression of you. But use emotional intelligence: if the manager would react badly, is under stress, or you need them to sign off a budget, raising it afterwards may be wiser; if you need support from around the table to change their mind, speaking up helps.

blocks.text: This one has no single right answer. Understanding the context, the mood of those around you and what you hope to achieve will guide your choice.

You should now feel more confident about facing key leadership challenges. You've met processes and models - Tuckman's team development stages, Brown's approach to team building, Kotter's eight steps, Lewin's force field analysis - that give a structure for planning action or insight into why people behave as they do. All these topics are widely researched, so you can easily find out more.

blocks.title: You should now be able to
blocks.text: recognise a range of common leadership challenges; reflect on challenges you have observed or experienced; describe ways in which common leadership challenges might be addressed.
Next week: challenges for leaders of the future, including technological developments and global change, emerging leadership styles and where to keep up to date.

blocks.q: In Tuckman's model, at which stage should a leader mainly mediate conflict, using their authority when required?
blocks.explain: Storming brings conflict and emotional responses as members push against boundaries; the leader mediates and helps them recognise each other's work styles.

blocks.q: Which of these are among the three elements that help a leader motivate a team? Select all that apply.
options: A clear vision you believe in
Communicating only with your direct reports
Regular, inspiring communication to the whole team
Leading by example and being visible and accessible
blocks.explain: The three elements are a clear vision, regular inspiring communication to the whole team (not just direct reports), and leading by example while being visible and accessible.

blocks.q: In Kotter's process, which step comes straight after 'Create a sense of urgency'?
blocks.explain: Step 2 is to build a guiding coalition of effective people to guide, coordinate and communicate the change.

blocks.q: According to Brown (2016), which is one of the three keys to a team-building exercise that creates impact?
options: Keep it as close to normal work as possible
Create something tangible, such as an action plan or decision
Make it competitive so there is a clear winner
Hold it only for new team members
blocks.explain: Brown's three keys: identify the impact you need, decide what type of 'different' you need, and create something tangible.

blocks.q: Development that motivates staff always requires attending a formal training course.
blocks.explain: Development can include work shadowing, a stretching new responsibility, implementing their own idea, delegated work or mentoring.

chapters.title: Week 7: The future of leadership
chapters.summary: How hybrid working, wellbeing, AI and collaboration are reshaping leadership, plus emerging styles such as authentic, politically astute and 'un-leadership'.

blocks.text: Welcome to Week 7 of *Leadership and followership*. Last week you focused on common leadership challenges - team dynamics and development, internal politics and change.
This week you look to the future: how global change might affect leadership style, and the new challenges leaders will face.

blocks.title: Lynne introduces Week 7
blocks.note: Lynne Johnson explains that this week you'll get 'future ready' as a leader: exploring what might impact most on leadership in the years to come, why the word *collaborative* is on everyone's lips, emerging styles such as shared leadership, and resources to keep you up to date with future developments.

blocks.text: By the end of this week you will be able to

items: describe how global change can impact on leadership styles
describe new approaches to leadership
identify sources of information to keep you up to date with future leadership trends.

blocks.text: Change is all around us, from global and political transformation to changing attitudes and ways of living.

blocks.alt: A desk with a lightbox sign reading #New Normal
blocks.caption: Figure 1 The COVID-19 pandemic has brought about a new normal

blocks.text: One of the most significant recent events for the global workforce was the COVID-19 pandemic and the remote working it widely enforced. The imperative to stay at home has gone, but **hybrid working** has become normal for many of us - and it brings new challenges for leaders.
Haas (2022) describes the challenges of hybrid work as the **5Cs**:

items: *Communication* - technical difficulties, but also the fact that some people are more comfortable speaking up over screens than others, especially where barriers of power, status or language already exist.
*Coordination* - remote teammates can be left out of small exchanges and minor decisions, which can grow to include more important conversations over time.
*Connection* - social as well as technical connections can be lost, creating an 'underclass' who feel peripheral to the work and the social life that bonds colleagues.
*Creativity* - collective and individual; home workers miss spontaneous conversations and the stimulus of a change of scenery.
*Culture* - if people (especially new hires) rarely come together, how is a company's distinctive 'feel' maintained, and how does it stand out in the competition for talent?

blocks.text: Haas suggests using the 5Cs as a checklist with your hybrid team: evaluate, analyse, plan and implement improvements together.

blocks.title: Match each hybrid-working challenge to its 'C'

pairs.def: Some people find it easier than others to speak up over screens
Remote teammates get left out of small exchanges and minor decisions
Remote staff can become an 'underclass' who feel peripheral and disconnected
Losing spontaneous conversations and the stimulus of a change of scenery
Keeping a company's distinctive 'feel' when people rarely meet

blocks.text: Studying healthcare providers working in hybrid mode, Oleksa-Marewska and Tokar (2022) identified four core remote leadership competencies that indicate 'readiness for the challenges of remote and hybrid work':

items: **Communicativeness** - especially crucial in communicating vision in remote work
**Credibility** - personal and professional; important in building trust and commitment
**Self-development** - 'being open to the search for new solutions and acquiring industry knowledge'
**Digital readiness** - 'an openness to technological solutions and a readiness to implement and use them in order to improve the work of both one's superiors and subordinates'.

blocks.text: Leading in a hybrid workplace is a developing topic to keep coming back to - the resources in Section 5 will help you do that.

blocks.alt: A pair of cupped hands holding a smiling face drawn on a piece of card
blocks.caption: Figure 2 Prioritising the mental health and wellbeing of employees is now more important than ever

blocks.text: As well as changing work practices, the pandemic had a significant impact on health. The mental health and wellbeing of employees are now more important than ever for leaders to prioritise.

Burnout is 'a psychological response to exposure to chronic stressors at work [...] characterised by high levels of emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation and reduced personal accomplishment' (Kumar, 2018).
blocks.title: Burnout

blocks.text: Burnout has become a common term for both leaders and followers. Kumar (2018) describes these signs:

items: **Affective** - irritability, oversensitivity, less emotional empathy with clients, increased anger
**Cognitive** - cynical, dehumanising perceptions of clients; negativism/pessimism; labelling clients in derogatory ways
**Behavioural** - violent outbursts; irritability toward clients; interpersonal, marital and family conflicts; social isolation and withdrawal; responding to clients mechanically
**Motivational** - loss of interest; indifference towards clients.

blocks.text: Physical signs are excluded, as they can be observed 'only on an individual level'.

pages.title: Do leaders spot the warning signs?

blocks.text: Using written vignettes, Pischel et al. (2022) reviewed leaders' awareness of the warning signals of emerging depression and burnout. They found that 'even under favorable conditions, only about half of the leaders recognized warning signals as a health risk.'

Leaders 'showed lower awareness during times of high stress and low autonomy and when followers displayed less clear warning signals.' Leaders need to understand how their awareness may be impeded, and training on common mental health disorders and early warning signs may be valuable.

blocks.q: Pischel et al. (2022) found that, under favourable conditions, most leaders (around nine in ten) recognised warning signals of burnout as a health risk.
blocks.explain: Only about half of the leaders recognised the warning signals, even under favourable conditions - and awareness fell further under high stress and low autonomy.

blocks.text: Wright (2023) suggests these strategies to prevent burnout in yourself and your employees:

items: Encourage an open and honest workplace culture.
Put specific HR policies in place - keep workloads sustainable and allow time to relax and recover.
Notice changes in working patterns, such as emails sent outside work hours.
Be aware of workloads and deadlines; notice when people ask for help.
Notice behaviour changes - mood swings, energy levels, interactions with others.
Balance work allocation proportionately.
Think about giving back time (leave or fewer hours) after a heavy period.
Signpost to support.
Practise what you preach - don't work at all hours and expect out-of-hours replies.
Look after your own wellbeing - your team will likely follow your example.

blocks.text: Having tasted life without the daily commute, many people decided to change their careers after the pandemic. This contributed to what is often called **'the great resignation'**, and many leaders have had to focus more on attracting and retaining employees. The same applies to leaders themselves - and to their organisations' ability to attract and keep them.

blocks.title: Decoding 'the great resignation' (Gartner)
blocks.note: A short video from Gartner that focuses on decoding 'the great resignation'. (External YouTube content.)

blocks.text: Developing a greater awareness and understanding of the issues facing your employees is a good place to start.
'Disruptive technologies' may sound intimidating, but the phrase covers many things you know well - from using the internet on your mobile phone to storing things in 'a cloud'.

blocks.alt: A pile of smartphones showing different colourful screens
blocks.caption: Figure 3 Disruptive technologies are more familiar than you think

blocks.text: 'Any enhanced or completely new technology that replaces and disrupts an existing technology, rendering it obsolete. It is designed to succeed similar technology that is already in use.' (Techopedia, 2017)
blocks.title: Disruptive technology

blocks.text: Păvăloaia and Necula (2023) name the five most prominent examples: **AI, the Internet of Things, blockchain, 5G and 3D printing**. This course concentrates on the one with the highest profile and widest reach: artificial intelligence (AI).
A guidance document from the Information Commissioner's Office and The Alan Turing Institute (2022) defines AI as:

AI is an umbrella term for a range of technologies and approaches that often attempt to mimic human thought to solve complex tasks. Things that humans have traditionally done by thinking and reasoning are increasingly being done by, or with the help of, AI.
blocks.by: ICO and The Alan Turing Institute (2022)

blocks.text: Examples: in healthcare 'AI can be used to spot early signs of illness and diagnose disease'; in policing it can 'identify potential offenders'; in marketing it 'can be used to target products and services to customers'. With such wide uses, AI is likely to have a significant impact on the work lives of many leaders and followers.

pages.title: Activity 1 The impact of artificial intelligence

blocks.title: Activity 1 The impact of artificial intelligence
blocks.prompt: Allow about 10 minutes. Consider what you know about AI and summarise how you think it might impact on leadership in the future - within your own organisation or more broadly.
blocks.model: It is easy to think of negative impacts, but Khatri (2023) describes several ways AI might positively influence leadership: accelerated decision making, better predictions of future patterns and consequences, more streamlined operations, enhanced collaboration, and development of technical knowledge and skills. As AI's impact grows, some decisions and ways of working will change, and as a leader you'll need to be prepared and able to facilitate their introduction. Innovation management is a complex field worth exploring further (e.g. Nieminen, 2023, 'Innovation Management - The Ultimate Guide').
points: AI could speed up decision making and improve predictions of future patterns.
AI could streamline operations and enhance collaboration.
Leaders will need new technical knowledge and skills.
Leaders must prepare for changed ways of working and facilitate their introduction.
There are possible negative impacts too, such as concern about jobs.
blocks.hint: Think about decisions, operations, collaboration, skills - and about how people may feel about the change.

blocks.text: When disruptive technologies transform your operating and business models and customer experience, the staff experience changes too. Your role as leader is to **embrace, support, promote and deploy innovation** while facilitating the potentially rapid change your team experiences (revisit leading change in Week 6).
Many worry about AI and jobs, but the OECD (Milanez, 2023), drawing on almost 100 case studies across eight countries, is more positive than expected:

items: Employment levels have so far remained steady with AI adoption, though job growth has slowed.
Robust demand for specialised AI skills is driving growth in AI-related occupations.
Job reorganisation is more prevalent than job displacement - tasks shift towards those where humans have a comparative advantage.
Job quality improvements - less tedium, greater engagement, improved physical safety - may be AI's strongest endorsement from a worker's perspective.

blocks.text: AI can also drive tools for virtual collaboration, such as project management or content analysis tools.

pages.title: AI case studies: check your understanding

blocks.q: According to the OECD case studies (Milanez, 2023), which is more prevalent where AI is adopted?
options: Job reorganisation - tasks shift towards those where humans have a comparative advantage
Rapid falls in overall employment levels
blocks.explain: The case studies found job reorganisation more common than displacement, with steady employment levels (though slower job growth).

blocks.text: As the global population becomes better connected and opportunities for collaboration grow, a leader's ability to **build productive relationships and share control** is increasingly important.

blocks.alt: Cupped hands around a glowing globe linked to many connection points, each a tiny figure in a circle
blocks.caption: Figure 4 Collaboration and partnership is increasingly important

blocks.text: The pandemic and new ways of interacting, such as hybrid or remote working, have added to this. Creating, developing and maintaining connection between people - team members, partners or clients - has become an even more important part of a leader's role.
Collaborative leadership has been around for many years but is particularly relevant today. Hank Rubin (2009), founder of the Institute for Collaborative Leadership, explains:
You are a collaborative leader once you have accepted responsibility for building - or helping to ensure the success of - a heterogeneous team to accomplish a shared purpose.

This applies whether you lead the team in person or remotely. In *Collaborative Leadership: Building Relationships, Handling Conflict and Sharing Control*, Archer and Cameron (2013) set out three critical skills and three essential attitudes:
Skills

items: *Mediation* - addressing conflict constructively and effectively as soon as it arises
*Influencing* - sharing control and choosing the best approach to influencing partners
*Engaging others* - networking and building relationships

blocks.text: Attitudes

items: *Agility* - forward-looking, quickly assimilating facts and asking incisive questions
*Patience* - calm and measured, reflecting on new information and giving confidence to others
*Empathy* - truly listening and being open-minded to others' views

blocks.title: Match each description to Archer and Cameron's skill or attitude

pairs.def: Addressing conflict constructively as soon as it arises
Sharing control and choosing the best way to persuade partners
Networking and building relationships
A forward-looking mind that quickly assimilates facts and asks incisive questions
A calm, measured approach that gives confidence to others
Truly listening and being open-minded to the views of others

pages.title: A manifesto for the collaborative leader

blocks.text: Archer and Cameron (2013) offer a ten-point manifesto:

items: Seek out conflict early - address it openly and with confidence.
Don't expect partners to share your objectives - look for common ground.
Collaboration is not a zero-sum game - invest in your partners' success if you want them to invest in yours.
Value and use diversity to find innovative solutions.
Only get as close and collaborate as much as the situation demands.
Look to the long term in relationships.
Listen hard, then show you have understood.
Be clear where the significant 'points of interdependence' are.
Engage others in your mission to be a collaborative leader.
Be authentic in all you do.

blocks.text: This is broadly a Western view, from a more individualistic starting point. Elsewhere, for example in East Asia, people have a more naturally collaborative/collectivist approach, stemming from a childhood focused on family and community.
What is your experience of collaboration?

blocks.title: Activity 2 Are you collaborative?
blocks.prompt: Allow about 10 minutes. Choose one skill and one attitude from Archer and Cameron's list. Reflect on when you have demonstrated them, or seen others do so, and describe your best example(s). If you have led both in-person and remote teams, compare: do you demonstrate the skill or attitude differently? Are you more comfortable in one context?
blocks.model: Being collaborative is an increasingly important leadership skill with many benefits: collaborative projects are more likely to win funding, your connections keep you better informed about competitors and context, and people in your network may affect your future career. Closer to home, creating an environment where your team collaborates well takes effort but is a key part of the leader's role - and even if you're not yet the leader, you can use these skills and attitudes to work better with others. The core skills are the same inside and beyond your organisation. If you struggle for examples, ask your boss or mentor about joining collaborative, cross-team projects.
points: Names a specific skill (mediation, influencing, engaging others) and attitude (agility, patience, empathy).
Gives a concrete example of when it was demonstrated.
Collaboration brings benefits such as funding, being better informed and career connections.
The same core skills apply inside and outside the organisation, in person or remotely.
Seek collaborative cross-team projects to build experience.

blocks.text: Some of your team may be excited to learn from overseas colleagues; others may see it as an unnecessary complication. Gardner and Mortensen (2015), 'Collaborating well in large global teams', advise:
Focus on commonalities

items: Remind teams of shared goals - why you're working globally and what each team brings.
Recognise interdependence - explain why success depends on knowledge and experience from other locations.

blocks.text: Symmetrise information

items: Hold regular virtual meetings to share information and personal experience.
Prioritise members with the right expertise and the cultural intelligence to work with global colleagues.
Combine meetings with virtual tours of each other's locations to set the context.

blocks.text: Being clear about what each team contributes shows why the collaboration is valuable, and seeing people in their own environments makes working with them seem less daunting. Awareness training on the cross-cultural context (Week 2, Section 2.1) can also reassure concerns.

blocks.alt: A seedling with three green leaves emerging from a crack in concrete
blocks.caption: Figure 5 New leadership styles continue to emerge

blocks.text: Leadership styles keep being developed, reflecting changing attitudes and priorities. In Week 2 you met established and more recent styles; this section looks at the latest research and approaches emerging to suit how society now perceives work and authority.

Leadership has become more concerned with supporting a **positive employee experience**, and styles such as servant, coaching, democratic and authentic leadership - some long established - are gaining traction.
Many commentators stress the value of being authentic in what we do and say - particularly important as people struggle to return to 'normal' after the pandemic. George (2003) explains:

Authentic leaders genuinely desire to serve others through their leadership. They are more interested in empowering the people they lead to make a difference than they are in power, money, or prestige for themselves. They are as guided by qualities of the heart, by passion and compassion, as they are by qualities of the mind.
He suggests authentic leaders demonstrate five qualities:

items: understanding their purpose
practising solid values
leading with their heart
establishing connected relationships
demonstrating self-discipline.

blocks.text: Understanding your purpose is particularly important for an authentic leader - a challenging process involving self-reflection and self-awareness.

Smith (2023) explains that your leadership purpose should not be the same as your company's vision or mission (you'll write a leadership vision in Week 8). It should reflect 'who you are as a person and how you bring those unique qualities into your leadership'. It is about your values and what matters most to you - your ***why*** statement: the cause, purpose or beliefs that motivate you daily.
Examples (Smith, 2023)

items: make the world a better place by helping leaders help themselves and their organizations
advocate for growth, freedom and prosperity through hard work, risk-taking and connection
create an environment where everyone can reach their highest potential.

blocks.text: To develop your own purpose statement, Boulard and Cashman (no date) suggest drawing a Venn diagram of three overlapping areas: **grow, give and gifts**.

blocks.alt: Venn diagram of three overlapping circles labelled Grow, Gifts and Give, with Purpose at the centre
blocks.caption: Figure 6 The three G model can help to define your personal purpose

items: **Gifts** - which two or three of your attributes are most valuable? How are they, alone or combined, unique to you?
**Give** - when you act on your gifts, who does that help and how? What positive influence can you have on a person, situation or the world?
**Grow** - what situations or conditions enhance your ability to act on your gifts? What final factor lets you give them more powerfully?

blocks.text: Your purpose sits in the centre. Keep it to one sentence: short, simple, memorable and useful.

blocks.q: According to Smith (2023), what should your leadership purpose be based on?
options: Your company's vision or mission statement
Your values, who you are as a person and what motivates you - your 'why'
Your current job description and targets
blocks.explain: Smith stresses that leadership purpose is not the company's vision or mission; it reflects your values and the beliefs that motivate you daily.

blocks.text: As internal and external interests diversify and divide opinion, Hartley et al. (2015) present a framework of **political astuteness** skills that benefit leaders and managers in all sectors.

Professor Hartley (2023) explains that political astuteness is about 'working with contest and conflict to achieve organisational and social goals'. Leaders use these skills in situations from 'dealing with people within their organisation, including factions and disagreeing tribes' to 'liaising with partners and in strategic alliances.'

head: Dimension
Skills
rows: Retaining a sense of purpose; knowing when to move fast on your agenda and when to hold off; picking up signals (trade press, colleagues, external sources) about what is over the horizon
Knowing who to work with and who to exclude to achieve goals; making alliances amid competition; knowing when to collaborate or compete; understanding organisations' differences in alliances
Seeing others' values, motives, interests and goals; understanding organisational goals and power structures; recognising the threat you (or your organisation) pose to others
Listening; encouraging people to be open with you; being curious and making people feel valued
Self-awareness; self-control; a proactive disposition - anticipating and developing the agenda

blocks.title: Activity 3 Are you politically astute?
blocks.prompt: Allow about 10 minutes. Look at the five dimensions of the political astuteness framework (Hartley, 2023) on the previous page. For each skill, decide: Y = I already use it, N = I don't, NR = not relevant to my context. Note which dimensions are strongest and which you could develop.
blocks.model: Political astuteness matters both internally (revisit internal politics in Week 6) and externally. The framework is a useful checklist, especially for a leader still developing strategic thinking. In Hartley's (2023) survey of 1,500 people, the most frequent learning opportunities came from failure or mismanagement: 88% learnt from their mistakes, 86% from on-the-job experience, 85% from handling a crisis, 77% from a senior manager's good example and 70% from observing bad behaviour by a senior manager. Use your leadership journal to reflect on 'political' conversations you've joined or observed - what went well or wrong, and what could have been done differently.
points: Rates own use of skills across the five dimensions.
Identifies strengths and areas for development.
Political astuteness matters internally and externally.
Most people learn these skills from mistakes, experience and crises.
Reflecting on past political conversations in a journal helps.

blocks.q: In Hartley's (2023) survey of 1,500 people, which was the most frequently reported way of learning political astuteness skills?
options: Observing bad behaviour from a senior manager
blocks.explain: 88% learnt from their mistakes, followed by on-the-job experience (86%) and handling a crisis (85%). Observing bad behaviour was reported by 70%.

pages.title: 4.3 Is there a future for leadership as we know it?

blocks.text: In *Dare to Unlead: The art of relational leadership in a fragmented world* (2022), Céline Schillinger argues that leadership styles that worked in an industrial society are no longer fit for a knowledge-based one. We need 'leaders who can gain a better understanding of the world around them, who can facilitate connections between different domains and areas of expertise, and who can enable us to change what doesn't work.'
She suggests focusing on three 'universal values':

items: **Liberty** - giving individuals freedom to exercise judgement and develop their agency
**Equality** - embracing collective working practices and encouraging peer leadership
**Fraternity** - inspiring shared commitment to a common cause, forming communities based on intent and impact.

blocks.text: This view of leadership is a toxic ideology. It hurts people, it hurts organizations, it hurts the planet. It is time to 'un-lead': to realize that leadership is first and foremost a collective capacity to be cultivated, whose basic constituent is the relational and emotional fluency [...] including effacing oneself in the collective rather than standing above it. This requires not less effort than the traditional conception of leadership, but more.

Schillinger argues organisations 'make us sick' because we keep putting leaders on a pedestal, attributing singular virtues of charisma or 'natural' authority. Un-leadership, she says, creates sustainable economic and human value, unlike the extractive model we are used to.
A podcast associated with the book features Schillinger and other influential voices: weneedsocial.com/podcast

pages.title: Video: the leaders of the future

blocks.text: Rebecca Fielding shares her view of the types of leaders organisations will recruit in future.

blocks.title: Rebecca Fielding on future leaders
blocks.note: Fielding sees fewer permanent pyramid hierarchies (senior leader, middle and first-line managers, 'the troops'); fewer people, especially younger generations, want to work that way. Instead, as in Silicon Valley, people come together in fluid, non-hierarchical, project- and matrix-based teams: you lead one project, I lead the next because I have the expertise, then the team disassembles. This makes better use of individual talents. Alongside this, jobs for life are giving way to freelancing and the gig economy. So command-and-control skills ('I decide, you do') become less relevant; leaders need to engage people, use followership skills (delivering on promises, valuing others' talents), be agile and flexible, and bring networks together to work fluidly, creatively and at a distance.

blocks.q: Rebecca Fielding predicts that traditional command-and-control skills will become more important for future leaders.
blocks.explain: She argues they become much less relevant; engaging people, followership skills and agility in fluid, project-based teams matter more.

blocks.text: Some organisations are exploring alternatives to traditional leadership. Shared leadership is one; a more extreme model is **holacracy**, used by more than 200 organisations worldwide in sectors from education and technology to retail and design (Holacracy Foundation, 2023).
HolacracyOne describes it as a management framework with five modules, ideally adopted together but possible separately:

items: **Clear organisational structure** - no need to ask your manager who to talk to in another department.
**Clear rules of cooperation** - on transparency, prioritisation and processing requests.
**Efficient, 'tactical' meetings** - staying focused, avoiding tangents and time wasted seeking consensus.
**Distributed authority** - clear boundaries within which employees lead and use their judgement.
**Decentralised governance process** - anyone can propose changes to their own and colleagues' roles.

blocks.text: Online shoe retailer Zappos removed its management hierarchy and introduced holacracy several years ago. The focus was **transparency and adaptability**: tools helped staff identify the work that needed doing, and staff could pitch for work that interested them rather than follow an out-of-date job description.

In a *Harvard Business Review IdeaCast*, Bernstein and Bunch (2016) described the significant work of retraining staff and building the technology and structures. Crucially, it wasn't 'leaderless' - leadership was **distributed** throughout the organisation.

It isn't for everyone: a number of employees reportedly resigned soon after implementation. Zhou (2023) found self-management can enhance engagement and consistency in achieving objectives, but warned that intercultural collaboration and motivation need attention. Zappos now shares resources, testimonials and tours through 'Zappos Insights'.

blocks.q: At Zappos, holacracy created a completely leaderless organisation.
blocks.explain: Bernstein and Bunch (2016) stressed it was not 'leaderless' - leadership or management was distributed throughout the organisation.

blocks.title: Activity 4 What do you predict?
blocks.prompt: Allow about 30 minutes. 1. Find an article, blog or paper about the future of business leadership that captures your imagination (or visit the Holacracy website, or read about Schillinger's Dare to Unlead approach) and summarise it. 2a. How does that approach compare with leadership you've experienced or observed, or your own style? 2b. Could it be effective in your workplace?
blocks.model: Cutting-edge approaches like the one Zappos introduced are still relatively unusual, but interest is growing all the time. A radical change may be unlikely in your organisation, but elements of these new approaches could inform small changes. Use your leadership journal to identify areas that interest you and experiment with ideas.
points: Summarises a specific future-of-leadership approach or source.
Compares it with leadership experienced, observed or own style.
Judges realistically whether it could work in own workplace.
Radical change is unlikely, but elements could inform small changes.
Uses the leadership journal to experiment with ideas.

blocks.text: Leadership and followership have stimulated research and discussion for decades - and will continue to do so. If you plan to keep learning beyond this course, these resources may help (web links are in the course references).

blocks.title: Activity 5 Reviewing the resources - what works for you?
blocks.prompt: Allow about 1 hour. Spend time online reviewing the resources, organisations and individuals in this section. Some are academic, others practical - which suit you? Choose three resources you could regularly refer to or follow on social media, and say why.

Following people or organisations on social media (e.g. Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn) is an easy way to keep up to date with their views and activities without spending lots of time reading.

blocks.text: Welcome to Week 8 - you've almost finished the course! Last week you looked at how leadership is changing. This week you concentrate on your own leadership learning and development: reflecting on what you've learned and setting goals for your career progression.

blocks.title: Lynne introduces Week 8

Use your leadership journal from Week 3 to plan your leadership development; get networking once you've worked out who the right people are; decide whether you need further training or retraining; and decide how to progress your career - new responsibilities, a promotion, even a change of job? Review your personal aims from Week 1 and use all your learning to set you on course for the next stage of your career.

blocks.text: This course has covered a wide range of topics on leadership and followership. Some themes will be more familiar than others, but each week should have offered relevant ideas.

By now you should feel more comfortable with reflection. Your leadership journal should be well underway, you should have settled on a good time of day to add to it, and you should be developing a style that suits you.
Leadership expert Professor Jean Hartley is very clear on the benefits of a reflective approach.

blocks.title: Jean Hartley on reflection
blocks.note: Reflection is 'absolutely at the core of leadership development' - almost every course or workshop includes it. For the experienced, effective leaders Hartley has worked with, reflection is a habit of mind: they monitor themselves continuously, sometimes formally (a journal or diary, jotting points, talking with trusted friends). Leadership benefits from 'rehearsal', and reflection is that rehearsal: rerun a meeting or presentation in your head and write it down. You can reflect several times - first from your own position (How did I start? Did I get the purpose across succinctly?), then from the listener's (How did I come across? What was going on for the person on their phone?). Reflect with trusted others too, asking 'How did I do?' rather than 'Was I good enough?' so you don't betray a lack of confidence.

blocks.q: Jean Hartley suggests asking trusted colleagues 'Do you think I did good enough?' to get the most useful feedback.
blocks.explain: She advises asking 'How did I do?' instead, so that you don't come across as underconfident.

blocks.title: Activity 1 Reviewing your learning
blocks.prompt: Allow about 40 minutes. Review your journal entries, notes and activity responses from throughout the course. What have been your key learning points from each week? Two or three bullet points per week are enough to crystallise your thinking. If you've done this weekly already, bring those thoughts together here.
blocks.model: Summarising your learning points shows how your knowledge of leadership and followership has grown over the last eight weeks. This should be inspiring - if you can learn something new from 24 hours of study, just think what you can achieve during your career!
points: Lists two or three key points for each week.
Draws on journal entries and earlier activity answers.
Shows how understanding of leadership and followership has developed.
Notes what to take forward into practice.
blocks.hint: Weeks: 1 starting point and definitions; 2 styles; 3 skills; 4 poor leadership; 5 followership; 6 challenges; 7 the future.

blocks.text: You now understand more clearly what a leader is, the crucial interdependence between leaders and followers, and the challenges leaders face now and in future. You must decide how you want to progress from here.
Look back at Week 1, Activity 5, where you considered your aspirations for the course. Have they changed?

Before setting goals, many business experts highlight the value of a **personal leadership vision**. Knowing what kind of leader you want to be, and how you want to lead, helps you prioritise goals and gives you a clearer target.

pages.title: Activity 2 What is your leadership vision?

blocks.text: In Week 7 you considered your leadership purpose - 'your ultimate reason for doing what you do every day' (Robbins, no date). That can inform your vision for the future. Examples:
To be a teacher. And to be known for inspiring my students to be more than they thought they could be.
To be an honest and accessible leader, known for leading engaged and effective teams.

blocks.title: Activity 2 What is your leadership vision?
blocks.prompt: Allow about 15 minutes. Using your leadership journal, consider your own leadership vision. Keep it concise and inspiring: describe the kind of leader you want to be in, for example, five years' time.
blocks.model: Did you focus on personal traits and qualities, or on how you want to carry out the leadership process? Either way, you can start to consider how to develop from where you are now into that leader. A vision can take time to perfect, so spend more time refining it if needed. A mentor can be a useful sounding board.
points: Vision is concise and inspiring.
Describes the kind of leader you want to be in a set time (e.g. five years).
Focuses on traits and qualities and/or how you want to lead.
Links to your leadership purpose and values.
Can be refined over time, e.g. with a mentor.

pages.title: Activity 3 What could you do next?

blocks.text: With a sense of the leader you want to be, where will you put it into practice - your current workplace, a voluntary role, a new job? Take a few minutes to focus on the options you could explore next.

blocks.title: Activity 3 What could you do next?
blocks.prompt: Allow about 15 minutes. List all the career-related options you could potentially explore next - e.g. a new project role, promotion, a new job. If you're not looking for work, consider voluntary activities or sharing your leadership observations on social media. Include anything that comes to mind, even options you may not pursue. Categories that may help: in the workplace; outside work; in person; online.
blocks.model: This is a quick brainstorm of all the options available to you. You could include others - your mentor, manager, friends or family - to see if they come up with anything different. In Section 3 you'll edit these ideas and settle on key goals.
points: Lists many options without filtering them yet.
Covers workplace and outside-work options.
Includes both in-person and online possibilities.
Could involve others (mentor, manager, friends) in the brainstorm.

blocks.text: **Personal development planning** lets you focus on potential study, career and personal development options and goals.

blocks.title: An introduction to personal development planning
blocks.note: A short introductory video on the concept of personal development planning. (External YouTube content.)

blocks.text: You started this in Week 3, reflecting on your skills, those you'd like to develop and ways to develop them. The thoughts in your leadership journal are a useful starting point for your goals.
Make your goals SMART: **S**pecific, **M**easurable, **A**greed, **R**ealistic, **T**ime bound.
blocks.title: SMART goals

pages.title: Versions of SMART and other tools

blocks.text: The course Toolkit's Goal Setting tool uses R = Relevant and A = Achievable, and expands the acronym to **SMARTER**, adding Engagement and Reward. Choose the interpretation that resonates for you.

This course uses **Agreed** because you may need to agree plans with your manager, and **Realistic** because your goal must be achievable - you should have identified and be able to remove obstacles or constraints such as financial cost to you or your organisation.
Other goal-setting tools you can explore online include **HARD** (*heartfelt, animated, required, difficult*) and **PACT** (*purposeful, actionable, continuous, trackable*).

blocks.title: Match each set of words to its goal-setting acronym

pairs.def: Specific, measurable, agreed, realistic, time bound
Adds engagement and reward to the SMART letters
Heartfelt, animated, required, difficult
Purposeful, actionable, continuous, trackable

pages.title: Choosing the right kind of goal

blocks.text: Swann (2024) suggests different types of goal suit different circumstances; setting the wrong goal can be detrimental and lead to feelings of failure. Ask yourself two questions:

items: **Are you already good at the task?** If you have the ability and resources, a **specific goal** will probably work best - aim high!
**Are you new to, or still learning, a complex task?** A **learning goal** works better - e.g. identify a number of strategies to try out in order to get better at something.

blocks.q: You're new to negotiating budgets, a complex task. According to Swann (2024), which goal is likely to work best?
options: A specific, stretching target such as 'secure a 20% budget increase this quarter'
A learning goal, such as identifying several negotiation strategies to try out
No goal until you are more experienced
blocks.explain: For tasks you are still learning, a learning goal works better; specific, high goals suit tasks you're already good at.

pages.title: A worked example of goal setting

head: Stage
Example
rows: To increase my confidence in leading a team
Limited - led a university project group and captained the school football team
Taking the badged open course *Leadership and followership*; did a leadership module during my degree
Good communicator, empathetic, well organised, creative; limited experience of negotiation and strategy
More up-to-date leadership experience; build negotiation and strategic thinking skills

blocks.text: There are many templates for a personal development plan; this is one worked example (Table 1).

blocks.title: Activity 4 Putting it all together
blocks.prompt: Allow about 30 minutes. 1. Pull together relevant content from earlier activities (e.g. Week 1, Activities 4 and 5; Week 2, Activity 7; Week 3, Activities 3-6; Week 5, Activity 5; Week 6, Activity 5; Week 8, Activity 2). 2. Build your leadership development plan for up to three goals, using the same headings as the worked example: goal; current status (experience, knowledge, skills); development/training needed; action plan; outcome; evaluation; next step. Use your workplace's template if you prefer, and check each goal is SMART.
blocks.model: You may have identified more than one goal, in which case prioritise your action plans. Is it achievable to tackle them all at once? Don't set too many goals or you'll be overwhelmed and may not achieve them all, which can be demoralising.
points: Draws on earlier activities (aims, skills audit, style, vision).
Each goal is SMART: specific, measurable, agreed, realistic, time bound.
Records current experience, knowledge and skills, plus development needed.
Includes a concrete action plan and how outcomes will be evaluated.
Prioritises a small number of goals to avoid being overwhelmed.

blocks.text: A key element in achieving your goals is identifying people who can help - senior colleagues who can put you forward for opportunities (sometimes called a **sponsor**), or team members you collaborate with. A strong network can be hugely beneficial to your leadership development.
'The action or process of making use of a network of people for the exchange of information, etc., or for professional or other advantage' (Oxford English Dictionary, 2017).
blocks.title: Networking

blocks.text: Many people find networking daunting, but put simply it is about getting to know professional people and showing them your potential.

blocks.title: Networking advice (Harvard Business Review)
blocks.note: A short Harvard Business Review video with practical networking advice, including reconnecting with 'dormant ties'. (External YouTube content.)

blocks.title: Activity 5 Who can help you?
blocks.prompt: Allow about 10 minutes. Look at your goals and action plans from Activity 4. Who could help you? List: people you already know (at work, personally, including 'dormant ties'); people connected to them (LinkedIn contacts, friends, colleagues); strangers with a shared interest (leadership experts, forum members); and others.
blocks.model: Now you have a list of useful contacts, add contacting them to your action plan and set a time frame in which to do it.
points: Lists people already known, including dormant ties.
Lists second-degree connections, e.g. LinkedIn contacts.
Lists strangers with shared interests, such as experts or forum members.
Adds contacting them to the action plan with a time frame.

blocks.text: Several UK professional organisations have an interest in leadership (web links in the References):

items: Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development
Chartered Management Institute
Institute of Directors
Institute of Leadership and Management

blocks.text: Many run online discussion forums, conferences or other networking events. Your sector's professional bodies will also be interested in leadership whatever their specialism, so investigate their approach to leadership development too.
Outside the UK, use a search engine to find organisations relevant to your profession or focused on leadership.

blocks.caption: Figure 4 Training leaders is big business

blocks.text: Leadership development and training is big business: one report found US companies spend $14 billion a year on it. Many organisations offer physical and virtual courses promising key skills or knowledge.

This course has given you a taster, but you may want to learn more about key areas to meet your goals. You don't have to be a leader to benefit: **followers can gain as much from leadership training as leaders**. Followers are the leaders of the future, and a good organisation will develop them too.
Many organisations train their staff internally or externally. Before looking outside, investigate the in-house options. Contact Human Resources or talk to your manager. It could be:

items: a dedicated leadership training programme
a workshop covering a specific skill
an afternoon of networking with existing leaders in your organisation.

blocks.text: If nothing meets your needs, offer to organise something. Find out if there's a budget for external speakers, and consider opening it to staff across the organisation - a useful networking opportunity that might even help with internal politics!
You don't need a leadership qualification to prove you're a good leader. It can be useful, but it's no substitute for practical experience.
Choose a reputable provider: professional organisations offer or endorse programmes, and catalogues such as findcourses.co.uk give a starting point. Ask:

items: Will it develop the right skills and take me closer to my goals?
Is it practical, theoretical or a mix - what suits me best?
Do the content and delivery style inspire and motivate me?
Will I get regular feedback on my progress?
What support is offered - peer support, coaching, mentoring?
Will future employers recognise it?
Can I talk to previous participants first?

blocks.text: Research thoroughly: courses can be expensive. Ideally a course adds to your CV, builds your skills and confidence, and gives you a peer support network.
Leadership training courses involve many learning activities. Here is one example (adapted from Hart and Waisman, 2004).

blocks.title: Activity 6 Leadership shield exercise
blocks.prompt: Allow about 15 minutes. 1. Draw a shield on paper or in your journal and divide it into four quadrants: (a) two of your leadership skills; (b) the part of your current work you like best; (c) two values that influence how you lead others; (d) a recent success or accomplishment. 2. Which quadrant was easiest to complete, and why? 3. Which quadrant, if any, reveals something about you that others might not know? 4. On a course you'd discuss your choices with a partner or group - find someone to talk to about it.
blocks.model: Your background, values and personal philosophies inevitably affect the way you interact with and lead people, and this exercise highlights some of those characteristics. Did it reveal anything new? (Taken from The Leadership Training Activity Book, Hart and Waisman, 2004.)
points: Completes all four quadrants: skills, favourite work, values, recent success.
Explains which quadrant was easiest and why.
Identifies something others might not know about you.
Recognises how values and background shape the way you lead.
Discusses the shield with someone else.

blocks.text: To explore the academic side of leadership in more depth, many institutions offer relevant courses.
In the UK, the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (**UCAS**) has a searchable database of undergraduate and postgraduate courses (ucas.com).

blocks.q: Which statement about leadership training reflects the course?
options: Only people already in leadership roles benefit from leadership training
A leadership qualification is the best proof that you are a good leader
Followers can gain as much from leadership training as leaders, but a qualification is no substitute for practical experience
External courses should always be chosen before internal options
blocks.explain: The course stresses that followers are the leaders of the future, that qualifications don't replace experience, and that you should investigate in-house options first.

blocks.text: Congratulations on almost reaching the end of the course. Now it's time for the **Week 8 badge quiz**. Like the Week 4 badge quiz, it has 15 questions in total, drawing on the whole course.
To gain the badge you need to read each week of the course and score 50% or more in the two badge quizzes (Week 4 and Week 8).
blocks.title: Getting your badge

blocks.text: See the badge as an opportunity to reflect on what you have learned rather than as a test. Read each explanation after answering.

blocks.q: Kotter (1990) distinguishes management from leadership. Which describes *leadership* in his view?
options: Establishing direction, aligning and motivating people
blocks.explain: Kotter sees management as planning, organising and controlling, and leadership as establishing direction, aligning and motivating people.

blocks.q: Which is one of Bass's (1985) four 'I's of transformational leadership?
blocks.explain: The four 'I's are individualised consideration, intellectual stimulation, inspirational motivation and idealised influence (charisma).

blocks.q: Transactional leaders are process and action oriented, and can be particularly effective when projects must be tightly controlled.
blocks.explain: Their responsive, directive style gives clarity, though a lack of autonomy can demotivate.

blocks.q: Mayer and Salovey (1990) define emotional intelligence as the ability to...
options: achieve high scores on reasoning tests
monitor one's own and others' feelings and emotions, discriminate among them and use this information to guide thinking and actions
blocks.explain: Goleman (1998) later identified five competencies: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills.

blocks.q: Kellerman (2004) divides ineffective leadership into three groups. Which leader is 'stiff and unyielding, unable or unwilling to adapt to new ideas'?
blocks.explain: Incompetent leaders lack the will or skill; intemperate leaders lack self-control; rigid leaders cannot adapt.

blocks.q: In Kelley's (1988) typology, which followers 'think for themselves and carry out their duties and assignments with energy and assertiveness'?
blocks.explain: Kelley also notes that 'followership is not a person but a role'.

blocks.q: In Chaleff's (2009) model, the 'partner' follower shows...
blocks.explain: The partner gives vigorous support but is also willing to question the leader.

blocks.q: Shared leadership (Pearce and Conger, 2003) means that...
options: leadership behaviours are exhibited by a set of individuals, as a shared function rather than one person's role
the most senior person shares the decisions with the board
blocks.explain: It is 'a dynamic, interactive influence process among individuals in groups' - it relies on excellent communication.

blocks.q: Force field analysis, developed by Kurt Lewin (1951), is a change management tool that looks at...
options: the stages a team passes through
the drivers and resistors of change
blocks.explain: It weighs the forces driving change against those resisting it.

blocks.q: Which of these are among Haas's (2022) 5Cs of hybrid working? Select all that apply.
blocks.explain: The 5Cs are communication, coordination, connection, creativity and culture.

blocks.q: Which quality is NOT one of George's (2003) five qualities of authentic leaders?
blocks.explain: Authentic leaders are more interested in empowering others than in power, money or prestige for themselves.

blocks.q: In the holacracy model used by Zappos, authority is distributed so employees can use their judgement within an agreed scope.
blocks.explain: Distributed authority is one of holacracy's five modules; leadership was distributed rather than absent.

blocks.q: In this course's version of SMART goals, what does the 'A' stand for, and why?
options: Achievable - because goals must be easy
Agreed - because you may need to agree your plans with a current manager
Ambitious - because goals should stretch you
blocks.explain: The course uses 'Agreed' (and 'Realistic' for R); other versions use Achievable and Relevant.

blocks.q: According to Jean Hartley, why is reflection so valuable for leadership development?
options: It replaces the need for feedback from others
It acts as a form of rehearsal you can repeat from different perspectives
It is only useful after a major failure
blocks.explain: Reflection lets you rerun a situation - from your own view and the listener's - and you can also reflect with trusted others.

blocks.q: Which of these is defined as 'making use of a network of people for the exchange of information, etc., or for professional or other advantage'?
blocks.explain: This is the Oxford English Dictionary (2017) definition of networking.
